documents.t: An active artifact snapshot is the versioned runtime boundary for prompts, SQL pairs, user instructions, semantic models, schema RAG, MCP tools, and runtime policies.
QA Smoke is an explicit business check. It runs one real project-scoped MCP ask against the current Active Snapshot. Opening the page, refreshing Health, publishing, and startup do not run it.
| Operation | Meaning |

Before listening, the backend checks shared DB, chat provider, embedding, and pgvector through the same internal checker as mode=system. It tries at most ten times within STARTUPFAILFASTGRACESECONDS, logging each failed dependency. Exhausted grace exits code 1. Success proceeds immediately to configured IMPORT_DIR snapshot convergence; an invalid configured import also exits non-zero with its project cause.

If the process exits during boot, inspect its final log entry. It identifies the failed shared dependency and attempt number, or the configured IMPORT_DIR project and content error. System health is retried up to ten times within the grace budget; a configured import error exits non-zero.

Created: 2026-10-26 · Updated: 2026-10-26 docs/20261024_evaluation preserves the original files behind the BIRD baseline reports. The folder contains this README and evidence.zip; the ZIP keeps 549 source records together while retaining their original paths. Download evidence.zip (12 MiB) The archive is an audit trail, not another dataset or another evaluation run. It contains BIRD run requests, responses, scores, traces, Opik and Rhesis records, screenshots, source files, and the per-file checksum manifest. The evidence archive guide summarizes all folders and links to the related reports.

From a repository checkout, extract the ZIP into this directory: python3 -m zipfile -e docs/20261024_evaluation/evidence.zip docs/20261024_evaluation Then validate the extracted files with bird-evidence-sha256.json from the archive. If you downloaded the ZIP separately, use its saved path as the first argument and keep the same destination directory.

The runtime has one owner for each truth: Truth Owner Active prompt/knowledge package Active artifact snapshot Runtime execution sequence LangGraph pipeline External tool boundary MCP proxy and project tool definitions Startup operator state Startup-readiness service Process lifecycle Kubernetes probes and non-zero exit Avoid fallback composition across draft, active, and partially materialized state. If a required boundary is missing, surface the blocker and fail the affected operation.

Artifact version APIs manage the publish and activation lifecycle. The active response includes the artifact version identity, bundle hash, runtime identity, schema RAG binding, and data-source fingerprint. Use the Dashboard artifact review page for normal operator workflows. Use the API directly for scripted import validation, activation checks, and troubleshooting evidence. warning Do not treat an artifact row as servable until it is active, its runtime identity is consistent, and project Runtime Readiness plus QA Smoke are successful.

Created: 2026-09-21 12:48:12 +08:00 · Updated: 2026-10-12 23:54:03 +08:00 GET /api/health is cheap liveness; it performs no dependency or QA calls. For copy-ready checks with response samples and field explanations, see Check project health and troubleshoot. POST request Checks Response /api/health?mode=system Shared control-plane DB, one chat probe, embedding, pgvector .system, .errors /api/health?mode=project&projectId=equity Current Active bundleHash, derived material, query-side DB .project.qaAvailable, .project.runtime, .project.errors /api/health?mode=smoke&projectId=equity One real MCP Ask .smoke.status, .smoke.bundleHash, .smoke.ask /api/health?mode=full System once, then all projects serially .system, .projects[projectId].qaSmoke, .errors project and smoke require a registered projectId; system and full reject it. Invalid parameters return HTTP 400 before probing. Completed diagnostics return HTTP 200 with structured errors. Smoke is one attempt (passed, failed, or not_run), and a failed Ask does not change the current Active or project qaAvailable.

These commands call the local FastAPI backend directly on its default development port (4000). They need no request body. If your backend uses another port, use that port in the URL. The e2e mock backend defaults to 12345. Check that the backend is responding: curl -sS 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health' | jq . Check shared services, including the chat LLM, embedding provider, and vector-query capability. This makes one chat probe and one embedding probe: curl -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=system' | jq '{mode,status,failedChecks:[.system.checks[] | select(.status != "ready") | {key,label,status,summary,details,reasonCode,nextAction,diagnostics}],errors}' Check one project's Active Snapshot, Schema RAG, and business database. This does not run an Ask: project_id='fund'; curl -sS -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=project&projectId=${project_id}" | jq '{mode,status,qaAvailable:.project.qaAvailable,bundleHash:.project.bundleHash,failedChecks:[(.project.runtime.checks // [])[] | select(.status != "ready") | {key,label,status,summary,details,reasonCode,nextAction,diagnostics}],errors:.project.errors}' Run one real MCP Ask for the project. This is the no-UI equivalent of QA Smoke and may call the configured LLM. The health endpoint resolves the project's configured Ask tool and uses the MCP client internally; you do not need to handcraft MCP headers or a session: project_id='fund'; curl -sS -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=smoke&projectId=${project_id}" | jq '{mode,status,smokeStatus:.smoke.status,summary:.smoke.summary,details:.smoke.details,bundleHash:.smoke.bundleHash,ask:.smoke.ask,errors}'
documents.s: Run checks with curl, without the UI

documents.t:
Use this when you want to test a custom question rather than the fixed QA Smoke question. First discover the tool name from the selected project's tools/list response. In the live equity project, that response lists equity_ask and equity_saerch_test: curl -sS -N --max-time 30 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/mcp/equity/' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \ -H 'Mcp-Method: tools/list' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"},"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}' The response is a JSON-RPC result with resultType: "complete"; the live equity tool names include equity_ask and equity_saerch_test. The full list entries also include each tool's description and inputSchema. For another project, replace equity in the path and use a name from that project's response. Then edit the variables below. The same tool_name is sent in both Mcp-Name and JSON-RPC params.name: api_base='http://127.0.0.1:4000' project_id='equity' tool_name='equity_saerch_test' staff_id='guest' qa='How many core business records are there?' curl -N -sS "${api_base}/mcp/${project_id}/" \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \ -H 'Mcp-Method: tools/call' \ -H "Mcp-Name: ${tool_name}" \ -H "X_ABC_STAFF_HEADER: ${staff_id}" \ -d "$(jq -n --arg tool_name "$tool_name" --arg qa "$qa" '{jsonrpc:"2.0",id:2,method:"tools/call",params:{name:$tool_name,arguments:{query:$qa},_meta:{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{name:"curl",version:"1.0"},"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}})" The live equity call produced an SSE event: message whose data: contains this abbreviated JSON-RPC response (generated IDs and long reasoning text omitted): { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "{
 "status": "success",
 "confidence": 0.9,
 "query": "How many core business records are there?",
 "results": [{"core_business_record_count": 1446}],
 ..." }], "isError": false, "structuredContent": { "status": "success", "bundleHash": "<Active Snapshot hash>", "confidence": 0.9, "query": "How many core business records are there?", "results": [{"core_business_record_count": 1446}], "sql": "SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT fund_code) AS core_business_record_count FROM fund_master_view;", "meta": {"mode": "SQL_EXECUTE_RESULT", "timing": {"totalDurationMs": 19939}}, "reason": {"answer": "<answer explanation>", "business": "<business reasoning>", "technical": "<technical analysis>"}, "queryId": "<generated query ID>", "threadId": "<generated thread ID>", "traceId": "<generated trace ID>", "suggestedQuestion": ["<follow-up question>"], "groundReason": "<grounding explanation>" }, "_meta": {"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": {"name": "NL2SQL MCP Server - equity", "version": "1.0.0"}} } } content[0].text contains the historical business JSON as text, while structuredContent exposes the same result as an object for clients that support it. resultType and isError are MCP call status; structuredContent.status is the NL2SQL business outcome. The live count, hash, IDs and reasoning vary by request and Active Snapshot. This is the project's current stateless MCP request shape. It does not need an initialize request or Mcp-Session-Id. The selected project and tool name must exist in the active MCP configuration. For all registered projects, run the shared checks once and then project checks and Smoke serially: curl -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=full' | jq '{mode,status,systemStatus:.system.status,projects:[.projects[] | {projectId,status,qaAvailable,smokeStatus:.qaSmoke.status,smokeDetails:.qaSmoke.details}],errors}' full waits for the complete report and can run one Ask for each project whose runtime is ready. Use it for manual troubleshooting, not as a startup, liveness, or Kubernetes probe. The default identity is guest; to send a staff identity, use the configured HTTP_STAFF_HEADER header. For the default local header, that is X_ABC_STAFF_HEADER. Read the returned JSON status, not just curl's exit code: a completed diagnostic can return HTTP 200 with a non-ready status such as failed, partial, or setup. For an LLM/Ask failure, inspect .smoke.details and .smoke.ask.details; for runtime failures, inspect the failed check's details, reasonCode, and nextAction. Keep -f off curl so it does not hide a structured error response. Unpublished changes are inspected separately with GET /api/artifact-versions/freshness?projectId=equity.

documents.t: Execute one natural-language question against a registered project. POST /api/nl2sql?projectId=equity Content-Type: application/json { "query": "What is the total fund count?", "recordsLimit": 50 } projectId is required. Change it to fund or another registered project to run against that project's active runtime. The API does not select a default project.

{ "status": "success", "confidence": 0.9, "query": "What is the total fund count?", "queryId": "...", "threadId": "...", "traceId": "...", "sql": "SELECT COUNT(*) ...", "results": [{"total": 5}], "meta": {}, "reason": {}, "suggestedQuestion": [], "groundReason": "" } The HTTP API and MCP nl2sql tool use the same backend execution flow and active snapshot. The HTTP API does not call the MCP endpoint.

Missing or unknown projectId: client error; no query starts. Missing or empty query: validation error; no query starts. Runtime readiness or stale active snapshot: explicit readiness error; no fallback configuration is used.

Created: 2026-09-21 · Updated: 2026-10-12 MCP exposes project-scoped tools such as ask and nl2sql at /mcp/{projectId}/. The server loads tool definitions from the project's Active Snapshot. Modern product calls use MCP 2026-07-28 without a Session ID; the official SDK handles older third-party clients at the same endpoint. The FastAPI lifespan owns each project's SDK session manager. Publish changes the Active bundleHash; the next request updates that project's tool definitions in the existing MCP server, so an in-flight request can finish with the bundle it started with. Frontend / QA Smoke (project selected) ↓ Backend MCP proxy ↓ Project tool definition ↓ MCP tools/call or resources/read ↓ Structured result with the Active bundleHash QA Smoke uses the same project runtime path as user QA and therefore catches tool, provider, snapshot, and schema problems together.

Older clients can keep their existing initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/call flow. The SDK returns a real Mcp-Session-Id during initialization; include it and the negotiated MCP-Protocol-Version in subsequent requests. Sessions belong to one server process, so older clients need sticky routing when there are multiple workers. For successful NL2SQL calls, JSON.parse(response.result.content[0].text) returns the historical business object with exactly these fields: status, confidence, query, queryId, threadId, traceId, results, sql, meta, reason, suggestedQuestion, groundReason The values come from that same execution. reason retains business, technical and answer; result columns and business arrays keep their order. Older successful tool results contain content and isError, without resultType or structuredContent. Modern NL2SQL calls keep structuredContent, the same-run bundleHash, and the SDK's modern result envelope. Their text contains the same historical projection; shared fields equal the structured values. Ask remains a separate semantic tool with its existing structured result and progress stream. Failures have isError: true and safe diagnostic information rather than a success summary. Session support does not force every HTTP response to be plain JSON: retain the native JSON/SSE transport and decode it using the response Content-Type. The response regression is verified by e2e/mock-s10-nl2sql-mcp-contract.spec.ts in the existing 99 mock suite, using real HTTP sessions and an independent same-run history comparison. Historical expected values come from Git d03b3f3b and an isolated SDK 1.26 replay.

Natural Language to SQL (NL2SQL), also known as Text-to-SQL, translates a user’s natural-language question into a SQL query over a relational database. A reliable system resolves ambiguity, links the question to the correct schema, and grounds generation with approved metadata and examples. To reduce hallucinations, it validates generated SQL against the schema, restricts execution to safe read-only operations, and keeps the generation and validation trace visible. These controls make errors detectable and traceable instead of silently guessing. NL2SQL survey · Microsoft NL2SQL workflow

× Workflow at a glance One conversational entry point. Three specialist paths. UI Chat sends each question to the Chat Agent, which orchestrates routing and aggregation across domain-specific MCPs. Generated SQL — Attempt 1 SELECT fund_code, fund_full_name AS fund_name, equity_geographic_allocation_in_asia_developed, equity_geographic_allocation_in_united_states FROM fund_master_view WHERE equity_geographic_allocation_in_asia_developed > 0 ... Validate / Retry Candidate SQL, schema contract, dialect rules, validator/dry-plan feedback→Validated SQL or actionable error Retry and repair Check syntax, references, joins, grain, permissions, and read-only constraints before execution. Retry only actionable errors with a bounded budget. Validation feedback invalid: SQL syntax error invalid: UNION / ORDER BY clause Final SQL Validated SQL, trace, policy checks, execution limits→SQL, rows/answer, provenance, trace Execution safety + Eval Execute through a governed read-only connector with timeout/row limits and retain evidence for Golden NL-SQL regression checks. Validated SQL SELECT fund_code, fund_full_name AS fund_name, equity_geographic_allocation_in_asia_developed, equity_geographic_allocation_in_united_states FROM fund_master_view WHERE equity_geographic_allocation_in_asia_developed > 0; On narrow screens, swipe horizontally inside the table to view all columns.

LangGraph SQL agent tutorial: list tables → select relevant tables → inspect schema → generate SQL → check before execution → execute → correct actionable errors → answer. Wren correctness architecture: targeted retrieval, plan/validate before database access, governed connectors, and bounded correction. Wren Architecture — Correctness is a system: ambiguity detection, value profiling, generation trace, retry/repair, and evaluation as explicit correctness primitives. Wren memory system: retrieve relevant context and proven NL-SQL pairs before generation; store confirmed pairs after successful execution. Schema linking research: identify the subset of schema needed for the question instead of treating the whole database schema as equivalent context.

The runtime keeps the generation path explicit and observable: Each stage consumes canonical state from the current project and active artifact snapshot. The final response includes the generated SQL and runtime evidence needed to explain how it was produced.
Retrieval supplies evidence; it does not replace the runtime schema contract.

Layer Purpose Example Schema metadata Identifies valid tables and columns fund_master_view Semantic mappings Connects business terms to canonical fields US allocation → ..._in_united_states Similar questions Finds related user intent “Which funds have the highest US allocation?” Few-shot SQL Provides a question-to-SQL pattern SELECT ... FROM fund_master_view User instructions Applies project-specific policy Alias and formatting rules The active artifact snapshot binds these inputs together so a query does not combine a draft prompt, an old SQL example, and a different live schema.

Semantic mappings are the bridge between business language and canonical runtime fields. Key: metric Value: geographic equity allocation Key: region.asia_developed Value: fund_master_view.equity_geographic_allocation_in_asia_developed Key: region.united_states Value: fund_master_view.equity_geographic_allocation_in_united_states Keep the mapping explicit. A human can review the business meaning, while the SQL generator receives the exact field binding.

WDV NL2SQL is a governed query runtime for fund and equity data. It gives chat and agent clients a shared, versioned context, then turns natural-language questions into SQL, data, answers, and traceable execution evidence.

An LLM can write plausible SQL, but raw schemas rarely contain canonical business definitions, join intent, value meanings, or the active model version. WDV connects the chat experience to artifact-backed context, retrieval, validation, read-only execution, and MCP access.

A raw LLM query CLI Agents (OpenCode / Claude) WrenAI WDV NL2SQL 🧠 Writes or supports SQL ⚠️ often ungoverned ✅ through connected tools ✅ governed ✅ governed runtime 📚 Knows business definitions ❌ ⚠️ depends on prompts, files, and tools ✅ context + non-schema knowledge ✅ artifacts + metadata + SQL pairs 📊 Generates and deploys dashboards ❌ ❌ ✅ agent-driven ❌ 🔌 Works through agents ⚠️ depends on tooling ✅ native CLI agent workflow ✅ MCP + agent integrations ✅ application API + MCP 🗂️ Open, reviewable context ❌ prompt-bound ✅ project files and configuration ✅ versionable context + knowledge ✅ versioned artifacts + snapshot JSON file 🔒 Governed execution ❌ external or absent ⚠️ depends on tools and environment ✅ planning + connectors + controls ✅ EXPLAIN + correction + read-only + row limits ⚙️ Deployment · maintenance · architecture 🟢 LLM API + database/tool connector 🟡 OpenCode/Claude CLI + MCP/tools + project files 🔴 Next.js/TypeScript UI + Apollo GraphQL · Python/FastAPI AI Service + Haystack/LiteLLM/Qdrant · Rust/DataFusion Core + PyO3 · MDL semantic modeling 🟡 React/Vite frontend + LangGraph/Python backend A few distinctions are worth making precisely: Compared with a raw LLM query: WDV supplies an active, reviewable context and validates the generated SQL before execution. Compared with CLI agents such as OpenCode or Claude: CLI agents provide a flexible interaction surface; WDV adds a project-scoped artifact, retrieval, validation, execution, and provenance boundary. Compared with WrenAI: WrenAI provides a broader agentic GenBI surface; WDV focuses on governed SQL generation, execution evidence, and integration.

you want users to ask business questions through chat or an agent; SQL generation must be tied to an active artifact with a snapshot available and project context; reviewers need to inspect SQL, rows, validation, provenance, and trace; the same query capability must be exposed through an application and MCP.
you only need a one-off SQL experiment against a familiar database; your main requirement is an existing BI or semantic-serving platform rather than an application-owned NL2SQL runtime.

The dataset contains all 30 public BIRD debit-card questions. Inputs include official evidence and schema retrieval, without SQL Pair Knowledge. The model is mimo-v2.6-flash. Gold means the pinned reference SQL, with reviewed column-name mappings, executed on this POC database. Gold has not been independently certified as business truth. Observable result differences are separated from reference definitions that need review.

EX compares the set of complete result rows. Row order and duplicate rows are ignored; column order and every column value are retained. There is no automatic column removal, rounding, numeric tolerance, or answer correction. NULL is a database null value, different from zero and from returning no rows. Displayed values retain their recorded precision; display formatting does not create a new score. Result pattern (mutually exclusive) Records Interpretation Equal complete row sets 9 Pass on this data; not proof of SQL equivalence on every dataset Nonempty prediction with a different column count 15 Some target values agree; conditions, formulas, or granularity may also differ Nonempty prediction with the same column count but different values 5 1481, 1490, 1493, 1505, 1525 Empty prediction, nonempty Gold 1 1500, with an added transaction-month join condition Total 30 Zero final execution errors and timeouts; executable does not mean correct The 15 column-count mismatches are not 15 proven passes after column removal; semantic differences may coexist. Ask is the original system-request latency in seconds, including the existing retry for 1506. Source difficulty labels give simple 4/14, moderate 5/12, and challenging 0/4. These describe this sample, not an overall capability ranking. BIRD Soft F1 averaged 0.359453 on these same outputs. It gives partial credit for overlapping values in the actual and Gold result tables; it is supplementary and row-order sensitive. Use it to investigate a mismatch, not to replace EX. See the Opik report for score examples and the row-order caveat.

The execution pipeline completed; answer quality still needs work. All 30 questions have final results: 9 matching sets and 21 mismatches. Question 1506 retains its intermediate format failure and retry. Zero final errors does not mean no intermediate failures or correct business answers. Output contracts are a distinct area to investigate. Questions 1472, 1484, and 1486 calculated the target value but added explanation columns. Question 1533 matched the consumption-value set but added customer IDs. Question 1493 introduced rounding. Future work can investigate how to produce the requested fields, granularity, and precision. This run must not gain score through post-scoring column removal, added tolerances, or edited Gold. Calculation and data-selection differences also matter. Question 1479 omitted CZK filtering; 1490 used a different table and consumption measure; 1498 skipped monthly aggregation. Questions 1505 and 1525 primarily differ in counting records versus distinct customers. These issues cannot all be attributed to missing SQL Pair Knowledge or dismissed because the queries execute. Reference quality needs its own review. The following concerns can be checked directly against the questions, evidence, and SQL. They neither invalidate every BIRD question nor award additional passes. Question Reference definition to review 1481 Gold’s globally lowest monthly rows differ from the wording about lowest annual-consumption customers 1482 EUR filtering, the 2012/2013 denominator, and largest/smallest output differ from the question/evidence 1500, 1501 Gold associates transactions through customer monthly records without constraining the actual transaction month; one fails and one passes 1505, 1525 Wording refers to customers, while Gold counts monthly/transaction joined rows 1524 Station country is used as the reference for customer “nationality” 1526 Question amount 634.8 versus Gold amount 1513.12; evidence date also differs; Gold returns NULL 1529 Gold sums transaction prices after joining customer monthly records, repeating their contribution 1531 Top-spender selection and SUM(price/amount) differ from the question/evidence interpretation HOW TO READ THE 30% SCORE The supported statement is “EX is 30% against this fixed reference set.” It does not establish 30% business accuracy across real use cases. Removing disputed cases to report a better score would change the evaluation. A business-reviewed dataset should be published as a new version, preserving this baseline, and applied to all candidate systems with identical inputs and scoring in a complete rerun.

EX=0 · Fail · simple · Ask 15.5 s Question: What is the ratio of customers who pay in EUR against customers who pay in CZK? Gold result Actual result 1 row × 1 column: [0.06572769953051644]. 1 row × 3 columns: [2002, 30459, 0.0657]. Comparison: The customer populations match Gold: 2,002 EUR customers and 30,459 CZK customers. Generated SQL also returns both counts and rounds the ratio to four decimal places. Gold requests only the unrounded ratio. Analysis: The mismatch involves both column count and precision. The ratio relationship was understood, but 0.0657 is not an exact match at the recorded precision. 1471: original question, evidence, and complete SQL comparison Original question What is the ratio of customers who pay in EUR against customers who pay in CZK? documents.t: EX=0 · Fail · challenging · Ask 14.7 s Question: For the customer who paid 634.8 in 2012/8/25, what was the consumption decrease rate from Year 2012 to 2013? Gold result Actual result 1 row × 1 column: [NULL]. 1 row × 3 columns: [158447.52, 1079858.30, -5.8152426746723458]. Comparison: Generated SQL selects the customer with price=634.8, as requested, and returns both annual totals plus the decrease rate. Gold uses price=1513.12 on the same day and returns one NULL row. Evidence also states 2012-08-24, while the question uses 2012-08-25. REFERENCE DEFINITION NEEDS REVIEW Analysis: This is a clear dataset-consistency concern, not simply a demonstrated model calculation error. Original EX=0, NULL, and both queries are retained. Any corrected reference set should be versioned and rerun in full, without editing this baseline. 1526: original question, evidence, and complete SQL comparison Original question For the customer who paid 634.8 in 2012/8/25, what was the consumption decrease rate from Year 2012 to 2013? Official evidence '2012/8/24' can be represented by '2012-08-24'; Consumption decrease rate = (consumption_2012 - consumption_2013) / consumption_2012; paid 634.8 refers to price = '634.8' Gold SQL (read-only scoring version) SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTRING(date FROM 1 FOR 4) = '2012' THEN consumption ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTRING(date FROM 1 FOR 4) = '2013' THEN consumption ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN SUBSTRING(date FROM 1 FOR 4) = '2012' THEN consumption ELSE 0 END), 0) FROM yearmonth WHERE customer_id = (SELECT T1.customer_id FROM transactions_1k AS T1 INNER JOIN gasstations AS T2 ON T1.gas_station_id = T2.gas_station_id WHERE T1.date = '2012-08-25' AND T1.price = 1513.12) Actual generated SQL WITH target_customer AS ( SELECT DISTINCT t.customer_id FROM transactions_1k AS t WHERE t.date = DATE '2012-08-25' AND t.price = 634.8 ), yearly AS ( SELECT y.customer_id, SUM(CASE WHEN y.date LIKE '2012%' THEN y.consumption ELSE 0 END) AS consumption_2012, SUM(CASE WHEN y.date LIKE '2013%' THEN y.consumption ELSE 0 END) AS consumption_2013 FROM yearmonth AS y JOIN target_customer AS tc ON tc.customer_id = y.customer_id GROUP BY y.customer_id ) SELECT consumption_2012, consumption_2013, (consumption_2012 - consumption_2013) / NULLIF(consumption_2012, 0) AS consumption_decrease_rate FROM yearly; Trace lookup: question_id=1526; queryId=f442f689-482b-453a-83ce-da6aafd6d835. Comparison: Gold sums transaction price after joining yearmonth by customer ID, using yearmonth.date for January. That join repeats transactions across matching monthly rows. Generated SQL uses transaction amount for its total, yearmonth.consumption for January, and adds customer ID, producing different values. Analysis: amount and price are different measures. Gold’s repeated accumulation across monthly joins also needs business review. These reference definitions need review; original EX=0 is preserved. 1531: original question, evidence, and complete SQL comparison Original question Who is the top spending customer and how much is the average price per single item purchased by this customer? What currency was being used? documents.t: This page reviews one run of the current system. No other system has per-question results for these same 30 records here, so there is no evidence for a claim such as “this system answered more questions correctly than that one.” See the baseline guide’s external comparison for published versions, dataset sizes, databases, and execution conditions. This 30-question POC cannot be directly ranked against a 500-question Mini-Dev run or a full development/test evaluation. At minimum, align dataset and Gold versions, imported data and database type, question/evidence inputs, SQL Pair and other knowledge conditions, models and call budgets, and scoring rules. With the same 30 questions, retain IDs and report both-pass, current-system-only pass, other-system-only pass, and both-fail outcomes before comparing total EX, errors, timeouts, and latency. These records provide a traceable starting point; they do not establish an external winner.

Download all 30 questions, SQL queries, result rows, and trace identifiers · Download SHA-256 checksums. The archive retains the full original rows, including question 1500’s 976 rows and duplicates. Numeric and time values keep their original type/value encoding, and each record includes the original score-file checksum.

Created: 2026-10-24 · Updated: 2026-10-26 Rhesis baseline: 7/30 exact BIRD matches (23.3%). All 30 questions completed; there were 0 SQL execution errors and 0 metric errors. Mean BIRD Soft F1 was 0.2802. No human reviews are recorded. NO SQL PAIR KNOWLEDGE SQL Pair Knowledge: NOT USED. The Snapshot, actual retrieval, and generation inputs all verify this. Question only: BIRD evidence was not sent to NL2SQL. Gold SQL: scoring only. The Rhesis Code Metric receives it; the API request does not. Fixed evaluation data: a fresh POC project with 5 tables and 30 questions. We started with an empty proof-of-concept (POC) project, uploaded the BIRD debit-card data, published a queryable configuration, then used the Rhesis UI to send 30 question-only requests to the existing NL2SQL REST API. Rhesis applied the pinned BIRD Code Metric to compare each generated result with its Gold SQL. Measure Result and conditions Scope 5 tables, 423,050 rows; all 30 debit-card questions Test input Question only; no SQL Pair Knowledge and no BIRD evidence Official BIRD Execution Accuracy 7/30 = 23.3%; 23 result mismatches BIRD Soft F1 0.2802 mean; supplementary diagnostic, not the verdict Completion and errors 30/30 completed; 0 SQL execution errors and 0 metric errors Rhesis run duration 2m 48s in the UI; this is total run time, not mean API latency This is the question-only Rhesis baseline. The separate BIRD Without SQL Pair: 30-Record Analysis Opik reports 9/30 from an evidence-assisted run; its inputs and outputs differ, so do not combine that score with this one. The 23.3% result describes these 30 debit-card questions, not all business questions or the full BIRD leaderboard. For all 30 questions, the Rhesis verdicts, Gold and actual results, API proof, and SQL comparisons, open BIRD Without SQL Pair: 30-Record Analysis Rhesis. For the separate run with BIRD evidence as the judge's expected_response, see BIRD Without SQL Pair: 30-Record Evidence Rhesis. Its semantic categories are separate from official BIRD Execution Accuracy. The source records behind these reports are summarized and downloadable from the BIRD Evaluation Evidence Archive. This page walks through the POC setup, Rhesis run, official score, and external comparison. Screenshots and downloadable Rhesis records make the run reviewable without opening the local Rhesis service.
documents.s: BIRD Baseline: From an Empty POC to Rhesis Evaluation

documents.t: The project is bird_baseline_20261024. An administrator prepared a separate query database, an upload role, and a separate read-only scoring role. Business tables were then created through the product's upload interface. The previous debit-card project already contained tables with the same names. We preserved that project and used a new empty project to prevent existing data or knowledge from influencing the run. Initially, it had no Active Snapshot and no registered or unregistered tables with the target names. A Snapshot is the fixed business configuration used by this run. Every question was checked against the same version to avoid mixing configurations within one experiment.
documents.s: 1. Start with an isolated empty project

documents.t: Table data came from the official BIRD SQLite archive and was exported to five CSV files. Questions and reference SQL came from a pinned revision of the official PostgreSQL question set. Sources, checksums, and approved column-name mappings were recorded. All 30 reference queries were independently executed successfully against the imported database. CSV table Complete row count Columns customers 32,461 3 gasstations 5,716 4 products 591 2 transactions_1k 1,000 9 yearmonth: customer monthly consumption 383,282 3 Uploading table data makes the database queryable. Registering the evaluation dataset defines which questions to ask and how to score the answers. Question is the natural-language request. Evidence is the official business explanation or calculation hint. It is preserved for review but was not sent in this question-only run. Gold SQL is the official reference query. Only the independent scorer receives it; it does not enter the model request. SQL Pair Knowledge contains retrievable historical question/SQL examples. This run did not use it. “Question only” means BIRD evidence was withheld. The active NL2SQL configuration and its SQL Pair exclusion are documented in the run evidence.
documents.s: 2. Prepare table data and questions as separate inputs

documents.t: Confirm the project in Artifact → Schema. Open Guide at the bottom left and choose Schema & QA → Import schema. Click Import, select CSV data · POC, and select the five CSV files. This option imports queryable data rows; CSV model metadata only imports model definitions. Operation example: a passing screenshot from the current Guide, using the isolated poc_csv_reset mock project. It shows the entry point, not a result from this BIRD experiment. Click Review CSV and check each table's name, types, samples, and row count. We explicitly selected TEXT for yearmonth.date: values such as 201208 represent year-month strings, and the source stores them as text. Type choices affect query meaning and results; automatic inference needs review. The confirmation screen should show 5 tables · 423050 rows. Click Create schema to import the data and create a Draft. The configuration is not yet published for new questions. Actual run: confirm five tables and their row counts before Create schema. All imported values and types were checked separately; matching row counts alone do not prove matching data.

After import, Schema contains five tables, but the header still shows No Active Snapshot. Click Deploy to open the Snapshot workspace and review the draft. Deploy alone does not publish it. Actual run: the five tables are in Draft and the Guide points to Deploy. The yearmonth model on the right shows date as TEXT. Click Publish, review the content, then publish in the final confirmation dialog. We named the Snapshot BIRD debit baseline · no SQL Pair so it can be identified later. Wait until Current Snapshot shows Active. Actual run: review the draft and confirm publication. Import and Publish are separate steps. Read-only review after the run: the same BIRD Snapshot is Active with zero unpublished changes. Its identity matches the frozen run; it was not republished.
documents.s: 4. Deploy → Publish: move the draft to Active

documents.t: Open Check readiness from the Guide, then click Refresh report in Diagnostics. Active identifies the selected configuration; ready / QA available means the system can currently run it. A readiness check neither submits a question nor establishes answer correctness. Operation example: the current Guide in an isolated mock project. Readiness and QA Smoke are different checks. The actual BIRD readiness status is recorded separately; this image does not establish its score. Before evaluation, we confirmed the imported data, successful Gold self-checks for all 30 questions, and the published Snapshot. VERIFIED ABSENCE OF SQL PAIR KNOWLEDGE Snapshot: no SQL Pair entries. Actual retrieval: no SQL Pair selected. Actual generation input: empty SQL knowledge. Stages that did not execute were marked separately; missing records cannot stand in for proof of empty knowledge.

The Rhesis Test Set holds all 30 questions. prompt_content is the only API input; expected_response stores Gold SQL for scoring. BIRD evidence is not part of the Test Set CSV used in this run. The separate evidence CSV is for human review only. Download the Rhesis Test Set CSV The Test Set is bound to the existing NL2SQL API — BIRD question only REST Endpoint and the deterministic BIRD Official Execution Accuracy Code Metric. Each request is POST /api/nl2sql?projectId=bird_baseline_20261024 with {"query": "<question>"}; Rhesis reads the generated SQL from $.sql. Gold SQL and evidence are not included in the request. The completed run was launched from the Rhesis UI. Open the marked image · Open the original screenshot. Choose the existing NL2SQL endpoint and Fresh Outputs to call the API for each case. Choose Parallel and Test Set Metrics. The run archive records the configured concurrency, but the maximum simultaneous API calls was not measured. Preflight: No skips the optional UI checks; readiness and Gold self-checks were verified separately. Run the Test Set. Rhesis recorded 30 new API outputs and applied the BIRD Code Metric; it did not use an LLM judge.
documents.s: 6. Create the Test Set and run it in Rhesis

documents.t: Rhesis stores the SQL returned by the API and the metric result for each question. The official BIRD Code Metric executes Gold and generated SQL against the same fixed PostgreSQL data, then compares the complete results. A query can run successfully and still return the wrong columns or values. Question What the result shows Official Execution Accuracy Soft F1 1472 Gold returns customer ID 47273; actual SQL adds a consumption column. Fail 0.6667 1500 Official result comparison passes; the row-position-sensitive supplementary score is low. Pass 0.0370 1531 The returned values overlap Gold only partially. Fail 0.2500 EXECUTABLE SQL DOES NOT MEAN A CORRECT ANSWER All 30 requests and metric evaluations completed, with 0 SQL execution errors. The 23 failures are result mismatches, not SQL execution failures. Soft F1 helps inspect partial value overlap; it does not change the official Pass or Fail verdict.

documents.t: Open the Rhesis Test Run or the standalone 30-case Rhesis report. The report includes every question, the API proof, Gold and actual SQL, complete result downloads, and the official metrics. The actual Rhesis Test Run summary separates completed tests, metric failures, and human reviews. Open the marked image · Open the original screenshot. Rhesis result Meaning 7/30 · 23.3% Official BIRD Execution Accuracy: exact result matches for this 30-question run 0.2802 mean Soft F1 Supplementary partial-overlap diagnostic; not the benchmark verdict 30/30 completed All cases received an API output and metric evaluation 0 SQL errors · 0 metric errors The generated SQL and scorer completed; a result mismatch still counts as Fail 2m 48s run duration Total Rhesis UI run time; not mean API latency 0 human reviews Automated scores are not human approval Rhesis was configured for Parallel execution. The archived run does not measure maximum in-flight calls, so this is not a concurrency benchmark. Select a test row to inspect its question, generated SQL, Expected Response, metric reason, and review state; the Rhesis report shows these UI steps and screenshots.

The Mini-Dev → PostgreSQL section of the BIRD website and author reports were checked on 2026-10-24. The following are published reference scores; this run is not inserted into their ranking. System PostgreSQL EX Scope and key conditions SDIP + gemini-3.8-flash 69.00% 500 questions, native PostgreSQL; authors report adding rules after reviewing development/test failures, so this is not an entirely unseen-question evaluation FrontierSQL + gpt-oss-120b 56.80% 500 questions, one candidate, at most two repairs; test-baseline failures were reviewed during development Ontology2SQL 65.80% 500 questions; SQLite predictions deterministically adapted and replayed on PostgreSQL, rather than regenerated as PostgreSQL SQL Current Rhesis baseline 23.30% 30 debit-card questions, CSV POC; question-only, no SQL Pair, no BIRD evidence These reports use execution-result scoring, but question coverage, inputs, models, data ingestion and types, knowledge configuration, generation budgets, and development exposure differ. This Rhesis run sent only the question; BIRD evidence was omitted. CSV ingestion also does not recreate every primary/foreign key or index in the native database. EXTERNAL SCORES ARE REFERENCE POINTS, NOT A DIRECT RANKING This Rhesis run covers 30 debit-card questions in a CSV POC; the external reports cover 500 Mini-Dev questions. This run sent no BIRD evidence; models, data, knowledge, and generation/repair budgets also differ. The effect of adding SQL Pair Knowledge has not been measured in a controlled comparison. Percentage-point differences do not measure performance under identical conditions or isolate the effect of evidence, the model, or SQL Pair Knowledge. The case results point to output columns, filtering and aggregation, and numeric precision as areas to investigate; this run does not establish how much any change would improve results. A fair comparison can proceed in two stages. First, align published predictions to the same 30 questions, data, and scorer, comparing only EX from frozen outputs. To assess complete Mini-Dev performance, separately run the official 500 questions and native databases. Prediction replay cannot compare generation latency or replace the unperformed with/without-SQL-Pair experiment.

documents.t: Created: 2026-10-24 · Updated: 2026-10-25 The official BIRD result remains 9 of 30 questions (30%). The updated Opik suite adds a per-question Gold SQL comparison and passes 17 of 30 cases. That Gold SQL judgment agrees with the official result on 20 of 30 questions: it marks 9 official mismatches as passes and one official match as a failure. The official score remains the benchmark result; the Opik pass rate is a separate judge opinion. NO SQL PAIR KNOWLEDGE SQL Pair Knowledge was NOT USED by the NL2SQL system. This review preserves the original five-table pilot, questions, evidence, generated SQL, full result rows, and scores. The Opik run generated no new SQL. The updated test suite gives its judge each question's Gold SQL as an evaluation reference; the original SQL-generation run never received it. Read the baseline workflow for data preparation and the 30-question analysis for side-by-side reference and actual results. This guide explains how to inspect the evaluation in Opik.
documents.s: BIRD Baseline: Opik Evaluation and Review

documents.t: The separate Rhesis Guide: BIRD Evidence-Based Semantic Review runs the same 30 questions with BIRD evidence available to a Rhesis judge only. It explains the three judge outcomes, the 20/30 result, and why this semantic review is not directly comparable to official BIRD Execution Accuracy.

documents.t: Feature Use for this baseline What it establishes Datasets Store the 30 questions at version 1 Keep questions, evidence, and reference SQL together. The dataset itself is not a score. Experiments Compare the original run with a replay of saved answers Read the result and score for each question. The replay did not improve the model. Test suites Apply four automated checks to all 30 saved answers, including a comparison with each case's Gold SQL See which questions passed or failed and why. The comparison is judged by a model and is not official execution accuracy. Annotation queues Ask a person to review the saved answers Record human feedback. All 30 still await review. Opik supports automated evaluation and human review. See evaluation concepts and annotation queues. This guide keeps their results separate; it does not create a combined business score.

In the project sidebar, choose Evaluation → Datasets, then open bird-debit-f65faf4a-no-sql-knowledge-20261024. Select v1 and open Records. Search a question_id to inspect one case. Use Columns to show evidence, gold_sql, and question_id if they are hidden. The dataset has 30 items; its locked version is 01a16cdd-e44a-7565-b9d7-faa5dbb98333. The highlighted gold_sql and source_gold_sql fields are evaluation references. They were not sent to NL2SQL generation. Open the full-size marked image · Open the original capture. COPY THIS DATASET TO A COMPANY OPIK WORKSPACE Download the 30-question input dataset to reproduce the original dataset version. Download the Gold SQL review CSV to reproduce this frozen Opik review, including Gold SQL, saved SQL, and both result tables. In the destination project, upload the CSV through Evaluation → Datasets → Create new dataset. Use question and evidence as the task input; keep Gold SQL and saved rows as evaluation references. The input CSV copies dataset records only. The Gold SQL review CSV preserves the archived task inputs, generated SQL, Gold SQL, result rows, official scores, and assertion outcomes; it does not copy Opik experiments, traces, or review queues. See Opik's CSV dataset upload guide. Show the four actions inside the Datasets view In Datasets → Records, use Columns to expose or hide fields, search a question ID to locate one case, open Version history to confirm the pinned version, and use the dataset's Run experiment action only after a task and scoring metrics have been configured. This baseline replay links to v1 and measures stored outputs; it did not ask the app to generate new SQL. The dataset stores evaluation references; the original generation request and trace confirm the model did not receive SQL Pair Knowledge. The score comparison below uses this same dataset version. Test Suite v2 is a separate collection with each question, evidence, and Gold SQL.

In the project sidebar, choose Evaluation → Experiments and compare the original baseline with bird-opik-review-20261024-2038-gold-sql official metrics. The comparison link opens on the Results tab; choose Feedback scores to compare the recorded metrics. Return to Results to search a question ID and open its row for the saved SQL and result rows. Start with the original run. Its summary shows the complete-result match rate, average request time, errors, and timeouts. The original run exactly matched 9 of 30 questions. Zero errors and timeouts mean the requests completed; they do not mean the answers were correct. Open the full-size marked image · Open the original capture. Measure Recorded result Read it as Exact answer match 9/30 = 0.30 in both experiments Every returned row and column must match BIRD partial answer score 0.359453 average A supplementary score for overlapping answer values Average original request time 19,813.82 ms Time spent answering the original questions, not the replay task Requests with errors or timeouts 0 / 0 in the original run The requests completed; answer quality is a separate measure The comparison uses the same dataset version. The page rounds the partial-answer score to 0.36; the downloadable report keeps 0.359453. This replay reused saved answers, so it did not measure a model improvement. Open the full-size marked image · Open the original capture. The official exact-match implementation compares full rows. An extra or missing column changes the result, even if one value is correct. Duplicate rows and row order are ignored. THE PARTIAL ANSWER SCORE DEPENDS ON ROW ORDER The official partial answer score code removes duplicate rows, then compares rows by their returned positions. Row order can change the score. It does not prove that filters or formulas are equivalent and adds no numeric tolerance. Case 1506 returns the same 21 descriptions and passes the exact answer match, but its partial answer score is 0.190476 because the rows are ordered differently. Case 1533 is also affected by row order. We ran the official calculation without sorting or changing it. BIRD's Mini-Dev README describes this as a beta metric. Use it as a diagnostic, not as a business acceptance score.

Open the BIRD Gold SQL test suite, version 2. It contains 30 question records with their evidence and Gold SQL. Open the suite run results to search a question ID and inspect the saved SQL and rows. The highlighted fourth check compares each saved query with that case's Gold SQL. The suite applies all four checks once to each of its 30 records. Open the full suite screen. For this frozen replay, the task input is the saved question and evidence. The task output contains the saved generated SQL and result rows plus that case's Gold SQL. The judge did not call NL2SQL or execute either query. Gold SQL is an evaluation reference, not generation knowledge. The first three checks cover population and dates, calculation and grouping, and the requested answer. The fourth asks whether the saved SQL is logically equivalent to the Gold SQL. All four are natural-language assertions judged by a model; none runs SQL. The official result comparison remains separate and checks the complete saved result rows. Opik checked each case once and required one passing run. 17 of 30 passed all four checks; the dashboard rounds this to 57%. The Gold SQL comparison alone passed 17 cases and agreed with the official result on 20. The full list of results and reasons is available in the suite report. The amber column contains the per-question Gold SQL; the output column contains the saved generated SQL and rows. The 57% badge is the automated suite pass rate, not the BIRD result score. Open the full-size results image. The judge and official result disagree on 10 questions. It passed 9 cases whose complete output differed from Gold: 1471, 1472, 1476, 1480, 1484, 1486, 1493, 1528, and 1533. Most add columns or rows that the BIRD exact comparison counts as mismatches; case 1493 also rounds the answer. It failed case 1509, although the saved result matches Gold on this fixed database: the SQL uses a different date boundary, and the judge would not assume the two queries are equivalent without executing them. The judge has no database access, so this comparison is advisory. Show the earlier three-check suite for comparison The earlier suite did not include Gold SQL and recorded 26 of 30 automated passes. Its output is preserved in the original suite report. Version 2 keeps that run intact and adds the Gold SQL comparison as a fourth check. AUTOMATED CHECKS ARE NOT EXPERT VERDICTS The automated judge uses the same model family as the SQL generator, and its randomness setting was left at the default. It receives the question and evidence, saved SQL and rows, and that case's Gold SQL. It does not receive database structure, Gold result rows, or database access. It cannot establish execution equivalence from the Gold SQL text. The Gold SQL comparison still overclaims correctness on nine cases and misses one official match. For example, it treats extra result columns as harmless for questions 1471 and 1484, although BIRD compares the complete result table. For question 1498, the new Gold comparison correctly fails the saved SQL; the earlier three checks passed it despite the wrong monthly calculation. It also rejects 1509 because it cannot determine whether the different date boundary changes results on the fixed database. Keep the official result score as the benchmark measure and review disagreements with a person. Use expert-reviewed examples to check whether an automated judge agrees with people, as described in Opik's judge-alignment guide. Evaluation guidance also recommends combining fixed checks, automated review, and human review. This evaluation checks saved outputs; it does not run NL2SQL again. The task returned the saved SQL and results with the per-question Gold SQL reference and made no generator calls. The judge comparison is advisory; the official result match remains the regression score. The UI's Run button alone does not run this project's SQL generator.

In the project sidebar, choose Evaluation → Annotation queues and open the Gold SQL review queue. It contains 30 saved experiment traces from this replay. No human feedback has been submitted. The blank comments and feedback fields mean nobody has reviewed these cases yet. They do not mean the answers scored zero. Open the full-size queue image. Choose Annotator's view and Start annotating. Select a case, starting with 1472, then 1479. In Input, read the original question. Open the matching case in Dataset v1 or Test Suite v2 to read its Gold SQL. In Output, inspect the saved generated SQL, Gold result rows, actual rows, and official scores. The 30-question analysis shows reference and actual results side by side. Submit 👍 or 👎 and a reason only when the evidence supports a decision. Leave unclear cases unscored and add a comment for a domain expert. Use Trace to read the saved notes. This trace shows the generated SQL beside Gold and actual result rows. The Gold SQL text is available from the matching dataset or test-suite record. The feedback controls are still blank. Open the full-size reviewer image. Keep three results separate: the official comparison of returned rows, the Opik judge's four pass/fail checks, and human feedback. The partial answer score measures overlapping values and can change with row order. An automated pass is not human approval, and an unanswered queue item is not a zero.

Case Official result Partial answer score Gold SQL comparison All four checks What the records show 1472 Mismatch 0.6667 Pass Pass Customer 47273 matches, but the saved result adds a consumption column that Gold does not return. 1479 Mismatch 0.6667 Fail Fail The generated SQL does not filter for CZK, as the question requires. 1493 Mismatch 0.0000 Pass Pass The calculation is similar, but the generated SQL rounds the percentage and returns a different value. 1498 Mismatch 0.0000 Fail Fail The generated SQL returns a single record's maximum instead of the monthly total across customers. 1506 Match 0.1905 Pass Pass All 21 descriptions match; the partial score is low because the official calculation compares row positions. 1509 Match 1.0000 Fail Fail Gold and generated SQL use different date boundaries, but their results match on this database. The judge would not assume equivalence without execution. 1526 Mismatch 0.0000 Fail Fail The question, evidence, and Gold SQL disagree about the amount and date. This needs domain review. 1533 Mismatch 0.0741 Pass Pass Consumption values overlap, but the generated result adds customer IDs. The nine false passes and one false failure show why the Gold SQL assertion cannot replace execution scoring. The BIRD SQL test-suite research also notes that matching results on one database instance does not establish query equivalence across databases.

For a changed model or prompt, use the same dataset version, database, official score, and four checks. Review each question for changes. A different judge or different assertion wording can change the pass rate even when the generated SQL is unchanged. Keep the official 9 of 30 result matches visible. Do not present the 35.95% partial answer score, the 17 of 30 suite passes, or the 20 of 30 judge agreements as improved BIRD accuracy. External scores are comparable only when the question set, reference answers, database, evidence, and scoring rules match. This 30-question pilot is not a full BIRD leaderboard result. Request sent to the NL2SQL API: { "query": "For the customer who paid 634.8 in 2012/8/25, what was the consumption decrease rate from Year 2012 to 2013?" } Run proof: Rhesis status Pass · API success · execution ok Test result ID: a0fe7ab8-148b-41fa-be64-c39bbb727aba · API trace ID: 9670b425e554b3dc1bea55d2adac068e BIRD evidence NL2SQL actual SQL '2012/8/24' can be represented by '2012-08-24'; Consumption decrease rate = (consumption_2012 - consumption_2013) / consumption_2012; paid 634.8 refers to price = '634.8' WITH target_customer AS ( SELECT DISTINCT t.customer_id FROM transactions_1k AS t WHERE t.date = CAST('2012-08-25' AS DATE) AND t.price = 634.8 ), yearly_consumption AS ( SELECT y.customer_id, SUM(CASE WHEN y.date LIKE '2012%' THEN y.consumption ELSE 0 END) AS consumption_2012, SUM(CASE WHEN y.date LIKE '2013%' THEN y.consumption ELSE 0 END) AS consumption_2013 FROM yearmonth AS y INNER JOIN target_customer AS tc ON tc.customer_id = y.customer_id GROUP BY y.customer_id ) SELECT tc.customer_id, c.segment, y.consumption_2012, y.consumption_2013, CASE WHEN y.consumption_2012 <> 0 THEN ( y.consumption_2012 - y.consumption_2013 ) / y.consumption_2012 END AS decrease_rate_2012_to_2013 FROM yearly_consumption AS y JOIN target_customer AS tc ON tc.customer_id = y.customer_id LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = y.customer_id ORDER BY tc.customer_id Rhesis judge explanation The SQL correctly implements the requested business logic: the target_customer CTE filters transactions_1k on date = DATE '2012-08-25' AND price = 634.8, matching the question's 'paid 634.8 in 2012/8/25' and the evidence 'paid 634.8 refers to price = 634.8'. The yearly_consumption CTE aggregates consumption from the yearmonth table for 2012 and 2013 (LIKE '2012%'/'2013%') at the customer grain, and the final SELECT computes (consumption_2012 - consumption_2013) / consumption_2012, exactly matching the evidence's decrease-rate formula. Extra output columns (customer_id, segment, yearly consumption values) do not invalidate the answer per the criteria. The evidence mentions '2012-08-24' but the question specifies 2012/8/25, and the SQL correctly follows the question's date.

Question: What is the percentage of "premium" against the overall segment in Country = "SVK"? Request sent to the NL2SQL API: { "query": "What is the percentage of \"premium\" against the overall segment in Country = \"SVK\"?" } Run proof: Rhesis status Pass · API success · execution ok Test result ID: 8318391e-1c63-42bf-9290-ce6436834a90 · API trace ID: 03ad6fa926716b05d7a9807f5bd42dd7 BIRD evidence NL2SQL actual SQL No BIRD evidence was provided for this question. WITH svk_segments AS ( SELECT gs.segment AS segment, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, SUM(t.amount) AS total_amount FROM transactions_1k AS t JOIN gasstations AS gs ON gs.gas_station_id = t.gas_station_id WHERE gs.country = 'SVK' GROUP BY gs.segment ), svk_totals AS ( SELECT SUM(txn_count) AS total_count, SUM(total_amount) AS total_amount FROM svk_segments ) SELECT s.segment AS segment, s.txn_count AS txn_count, ROUND(100.0 * s.txn_count / NULLIF(t.total_count, 0), 2) AS pct_of_transactions, ROUND(100.0 * s.total_amount / NULLIF(t.total_amount, 0), 2) AS pct_of_amount FROM svk_segments AS s CROSS JOIN svk_totals AS t ORDER BY pct_of_transactions DESC Rhesis judge explanation The SQL correctly restricts the population to Country = 'SVK' via WHERE gs.country = 'SVK', aggregates transactions by segment (GROUP BY gs.segment), and computes each segment's share against the overall total using the svk_totals CTE (ROUND(100.0 * s.txn_count / NULLIF(t.total_count, 0), 2) and the amount-based equivalent). The requested answer — the 'premium' segment's percentage against the overall total in SVK — is clearly included as a row in the result set; the other segments returned are extra output rows, not an omitted or contradicted condition. Since the question does not specify whether the percentage should be by transaction count or amount, providing both covers the requested calculation. The expected response is empty, but the question fully defines the task, so missing evidence is not a failure here.

Question: What is the amount spent by customer "38508" at the gas stations? How much had the customer spent in January 2012? Request sent to the NL2SQL API: { "query": "What is the amount spent by customer \"38508\" at the gas stations? How much had the customer spent in January 2012?" } Run proof: Rhesis status Fail · API success · execution ok Test result ID: 6e0930df-0671-4ce8-918a-cc2ca07cb214 · API trace ID: 4123535ccbb9ec7ca6dff7158cfcb468 BIRD evidence NL2SQL actual SQL January 2012 refers to the Date value = '201201' SELECT t.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS transaction_count_at_gas_stations, SUM(t.amount) AS total_amount_spent_at_gas_stations, SUM(t.price) AS total_value_spent_at_gas_stations, SUM( CASE WHEN t.date >= CAST('2012-01-01' AS DATE) AND t.date < CAST('2012-02-01' AS DATE) THEN t.amount ELSE 0 END ) AS amount_spent_in_january_2012, SUM( CASE WHEN t.date >= CAST('2012-01-01' AS DATE) AND t.date < CAST('2012-02-01' AS DATE) THEN t.price ELSE 0 END ) AS value_spent_in_january_2012 FROM transactions_1k AS t JOIN gasstations AS gs ON gs.gas_station_id = t.gas_station_id WHERE t.customer_id = 38508 GROUP BY t.customer_id Rhesis judge explanation The SQL covers both sub-questions structurally: it filters the population with WHERE t.customer_id = 38508, restricts to gas-station transactions via the JOIN gasstations ON gs.gas_station_id = t.gas_station_id, computes SUM(t.amount) as total spend, and adds a conditional SUM for January 2012. However, the January filter uses t.date >= DATE '2012-01-01' AND t.date < DATE '2012-02-01', while the evidence states 'January 2012 refers to the Date value = 201201', indicating the Date column is stored in a string year-month format. Whether the DATE-literal range comparison correctly selects January 2012 depends on the actual Date column type/format, which is not provided, so the correctness of the time-range filter cannot be confirmed without schema review.

Question: Who is the top spending customer and how much is the average price per single item purchased by this customer? What currency was being used? Request sent to the NL2SQL API: { "query": "Who is the top spending customer and how much is the average price per single item purchased by this customer? What currency was being used?" } Run proof: Rhesis status Pass · API success · execution ok Test result ID: ccd0a8ff-72f9-4e9a-8514-c4b7d2da7ee2 · API trace ID: 01921cd5ec2ca15c556c424ef3a9a5eb BIRD evidence NL2SQL actual SQL average price per single item = Total(price) / Total(amount) WITH customer_spend AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(price) AS total_spent, SUM(amount) AS total_items, SUM(price) / NULLIF(SUM(amount), 0) AS avg_price_per_item FROM transactions_1k GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1 ) SELECT cs.customer_id, cs.total_spent, cs.total_items, cs.avg_price_per_item, c.currency FROM customer_spend AS cs JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = cs.customer_id Rhesis judge explanation The SQL addresses all three parts of the question. It identifies the top spending customer by grouping transactions_1k by customer_id, computing SUM(price) AS total_spent, and taking ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1. The average price per single item is computed as SUM(price) / NULLIF(SUM(amount), 0), exactly matching the expert evidence 'average price per single item = Total(price) / Total(amount)'. The currency is retrieved by joining the customers table on customer_id and selecting c.currency. Extra output columns (total_spent, total_items) do not invalidate the answer, and no requested condition is contradicted or omitted.

Question: For all the people who paid more than 29.00 per unit of product id No.5. Give their consumption status in the August of 2012. Request sent to the NL2SQL API: { "query": "For all the people who paid more than 29.00 per unit of product id No.5. Give their consumption status in the August of 2012." } Run proof: Rhesis status Fail · API success · execution ok Test result ID: 4da46d33-1173-439a-bddb-d4612bbbe496 · API trace ID: 5e5c935a73000c2d343623d47a83db9a BIRD evidence NL2SQL actual SQL August of 2012 refers to the Date value = '201208' ; Price per unit of product = Price / Amount; WITH product_buyers AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM transactions_1k WHERE product_id = 5 ) SELECT b.customer_id, y.consumption AS august_2012_consumption, CASE WHEN y.consumption IS NULL THEN 'No August 2012 record' WHEN y.consumption > 0 THEN 'Positive consumption' WHEN y.consumption < 0 THEN 'Negative consumption' ELSE 'Zero consumption' END AS consumption_status FROM product_buyers AS b LEFT JOIN yearmonth AS y ON y.customer_id = b.customer_id AND y.date = '201208' ORDER BY y.consumption DESC NULLS LAST, b.customer_id Rhesis judge explanation The SQL omits the core filter 'paid more than 29.00 per unit'. The product_buyers CTE only filters WHERE product_id = 5, selecting all buyers of product 5 regardless of price. The evidence explicitly states 'Price per unit of product = Price / Amount', so the SQL should include a condition such as Price / Amount > 29 in the WHERE clause. This changes the target population, contradicting the question's requested scope. The August 2012 handling is correct (y.date = '201208' matches the evidence), and consumption status is derived appropriately, but the missing price-per-unit filter means the answer serves a different population than requested.

End-to-end SDK implementation guide: deployment, WebSocket dispatch, a manually written entry point, and the docs-site data pipeline. The three metrics in this report run project-written Python code that adapts FLEX and calls GLM-5.3. They are hosted Rhesis Code Metrics, rather than built-in FLEX metrics or metrics created in the Custom Prompt editor. Rhesis UI launches the NL2SQL requests and sends each output to the assigned scoring function.

Receive the question, actual SQL and testcase reference. Rhesis passes expected_response to the Python argument expected_output. Validate the frozen question/reference and required content. Empty Evidence-only references stop here, before SQL execution or an LLM call. Execute actual and Gold SQL read-only on the frozen PostgreSQL data. Compare the complete results to choose the FLEX branch; this comparison does not decide the final semantic Pass/Fail. Build the adapted FLEX prompt with the real schema and permitted reference fields. JudgeClient calls GLM-5.3 to judge the actual SQL. Accept one boolean conclusion: true becomes score 1 and false becomes score 0. Exceptions remain errors; the audit records the actual inputs, request, reply and failure. Evidence-only uses private Gold to select the branch, but does not send Gold to GLM. Gold-only and combined read their judge-visible Gold SQL from the current expected_response. Each variant evaluates its own fresh NL2SQL output. ```", content)) if conclusions: if len(conclusions) != 1 or content[conclusions[0].end():].strip(): raise ValueError("Expected one final JSON conclusion") payload = conclusions[0].group(1) else: payload = content.strip() parsed = json.loads(payload) if set(parsed) != {"correct"} or type(parsed["correct"]) is not bool: raise ValueError("Judge conclusion must contain exactly one boolean correct input, "actual_sql": output, "actual_sql_sha256": digest(output) if isinstance(output, str) else None, "judge": self.manifest["judge"], "score": None, "status": "error"} try: if sha256(self.bundle / gold_sql=case["gold_sql_postgresql_poc"], evidence=case["evidence"]) references = parse_expected_response(variant, expected_output) gold_sql = case["gold_sql_postgresql_poc"] if variant == "evidence" else references["gold_sql"] with psycopg.connect(self.dsn, autocommit=True) as conn: conn.execute("SET default_transaction_read_only=on") conn.execute("SELECT set_config('max_parallel_workers_per_gather', %s, false)", (str(self.manifest["parallel_workers_per_gather"]),)) result = score_case(conn, output, gold_sql, self.manifest["sql_timeout_ms"]) record["execution"] = result if result["error"]: raise ValueError("Actual SQL execution failed: " + result["error"]) strict = self.calculate_ex(result["predicted_rows"], result["gold_rows"]) == 1 prompts = self.source.prompts(variant, self.manifest["schema"], input, output, expected_output, result["predicted_rows"], result["gold_rows"], strict) record["prompts"] = prompts response = self.judge(prompts) record["judge_response"] = response choice = response["choices"][0] if choice["finish_reason"] != "stop": raise ValueError("Judge response did not finish normally: " + str(choice["finish_reason"])) content = choice["message"]["content"] verdict = parse_conclusion(content) record.update(status="scored", score=int(verdict), correct=verdict, judge_reason=content) return {"score": int(verdict), "details": {"reason": content + "
Audit: " + record["id"]}} except Exception as exc: record["error"] = {"type": type(exc).__name__, "message": str(exc)} raise finally: record["elapsed_ms"] = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000 write_json(self.audit_dir / (record["id"] + ".json"), record) def main(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__) for name in ("bundle", "scorer-env", "opencode-config", "token-file", "audit-dir", "ex-evaluator"): parser.add_argument("--" + name, type=Path, required=True) for name in ("rhesis-url", "rhesis-project", "ex-sha256"): parser.add_argument("--" + name, required=True) args = parser.parse_args() args.audit_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False) manifest = json.loads((args.bundle / "manifest.json").read_text()) config = manifest["judge"] profile = json.loads(args.opencode_config.read_text())["provider"][config["provider"]] if profile["options"]["baseURL"].rstrip("/") != config["base_url"].rstrip("/"): raise ValueError("Judge credential endpoint differs from the frozen model") evaluator = FlexMetric(args.bundle, dotenv_values(args.scorer_env)["BIRD_SCORER_DSN"], JudgeClient(config, profile["options"]["apiKey"]), args.audit_dir, official_ex(args.ex_evaluator, args.ex_sha256)) from rhesis.sdk import RhesisClient, metric client = RhesisClient(api_key=args.token_file.read_text().strip(), base_url=args.rhesis_url, project_id=args.rhesis_project) @metric(name=METRIC_NAMES["evidence"], score_type="binary", description=f"{config['name']} reference-required FLEX-based LLM judge. Sole reference: testcase expected_response.evidence. Empty evidence is an evaluation error before SQL/LLM; no Pass/Fail. Gold is private branch context only. PostgreSQL/FLEX criteria and prompt diff are archived.") def evidence(input: str, output: str, expected_output: str) -> dict: return evaluator.evaluate("evidence", input, output, expected_output) @metric(name=METRIC_NAMES["gold"], score_type="binary", description=f"{config['name']} reference-required FLEX-based LLM judge. Sole reference: testcase expected_response.gold_sql, which must be nonempty. No evidence supplied. Explanations must cite the reference. PostgreSQL adaptation and full prompts are archived.") def gold(input: str, output: str, expected_output: str) -> dict: return evaluator.evaluate("gold", input, output, expected_output) @metric(name=METRIC_NAMES["combined"], score_type="binary", description=f"{config['name']} reference-required FLEX-based LLM judge. Sole references: testcase expected_response.evidence and gold_sql; Gold SQL must be nonempty. Empty source evidence stays empty; Gold remains available. Explanations must cite supplied references and disclose conflicts.") def combined(input: str, output: str, expected_output: str) -> dict: return evaluator.evaluate("combined", input, output, expected_output) client.connect() if __name__ == "__main__": main() The displayed source matches the archived file and the repository's evaluated implementation byte for byte. It reads credentials from private files; no API key or database connection string is included in the published source.

This is an adapted FLEX implementation. The code changes SQLite assumptions to PostgreSQL, removes unrelated school hints and unavailable-Gold instructions, requires a usable expected_response, and validates the final boolean response. The full source-to-runtime diff is available for review. Previous behavior Current behavior A matching CSV string such as {"evidence":""} could reach the judge Usable reference content is required; empty Evidence-only references stop with an explicit error. Judge-visible reference content was read from the private case manifest after a CSV equality check The prompt's sole answer/business reference is parsed from the actual validated expected_response. No-Gold prompts still requested comparison against an absent Ground Truth query Evidence-only instructions refer to the supplied evidence; unavailable reference-query/result comparisons are removed. A judge could invent a “typical” Ground Truth in its explanation All prompts prohibit inventing missing references and require an explanation grounded in supplied fields. The raw response remains visible for review. This is an explicit reference-required adaptation of FLEX, not an unchanged reproduction of the published metric. The new prerequisite does not create a business Pass rule. Source evidence/Gold are not rewritten, no numerical tolerance is introduced, and no alternate model or silent retry is used. documents.t: FLEX, Kim et al., NAACL 2025, uses an LLM to review SQL semantics because exact execution matching can accept a coincidentally correct answer or reject a useful answer whose result shape differs. The full method supplies question, schema, predicted/reference SQL and evidence; it adds both execution results when the results differ. Its correctness criteria cover population filters, joins, calculation, NULLs and output differences. The original implementations are full FLEX, NoHint and NoGroundTruth. We retain their correctness criteria and result formatting, with documented PostgreSQL and reference-input adaptations. Evidence-only still uses private Gold only to select the execution branch; the judge never receives Gold SQL, Gold results or an explicit match hint in that variant. The paper reports 87.04 Cohen's kappa with experts for full FLEX. That is agreement with human labels, not an 87.04% SQL correctness rate, and it does not validate the GLM-based reference-required runs on this page. Download the published paper · Pinned source and checksums.

Question: What is the ratio of customers who pay in EUR against customers who pay in CZK? Analysis: All three outputs contain the EUR/CZK customer ratio plus count columns; Gold-only and combined also round the ratio. The judges accept these presentation differences, while complete result matching fails. Check whether the consuming application needs only the ratio column. Stored expected_response JSON { "evidence": "ratio of customers who pay in EUR against customers who pay in CZK = count(Currency = 'EUR') / count(Currency = 'CZK')." } SELECT CAST(COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE currency = 'EUR') AS DECIMAL) / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE currency = 'CZK'), 0) AS eur_to_czk_ratio, COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE currency = 'EUR') AS eur_customers, COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE currency = 'CZK') AS czk_customers FROM customers Judge: Called · 1 (Pass) · Native Rhesis: ok / pass · Execution branch: Different results LLM judge reasoning The Prediction Query correctly implements the business rule in expected_response.evidence: it counts customers with currency='EUR' and currency='CZK' and computes their ratio as EUR/CZK.
