documents.t: All three files total 624 bytes and contain 22 rows. CSV file Rows Columns singer.csv 6 Singer_ID, Name, Country, Song_Name, Song_release_year, Age, Is_male singer_in_concert.csv 10 concert_ID, Singer_ID concert.csv 6 concert_ID, concert_Name, Theme, Stadium_ID, Year Download the official question and gold SQL record. On this page, select a CSV link to download that table. These are exports from the official SQLite database.

Database: concert_singer · Development record: 37 Question List all singer names in concerts in year 2014. Gold SQL SELECT T2.name FROM singer_in_concert AS T1 JOIN singer AS T2 ON T1.singer_id = T2.singer_id JOIN concert AS T3 ON T1.concert_id = T3.concert_id WHERE T3.year = 2014 The source SQLite query returns six rows. Justin Brown appears twice because the gold SQL does not use DISTINCT.

Open the local development guide and start the app with a project configured for POC_CSV_SQL_EXECUTE_RESULT. Open Schema → CSV data and select singer.csv, singer_in_concert.csv, and concert.csv together. Click Review CSV. Check the generated table names, normalized column names, inferred PostgreSQL types, and sample values. Change a type or name if needed. If the project already has tables with these names, delete those tables from CSV tables in this project before importing again; this workflow does not overwrite or update an existing table. Click Create tables and import. After import, confirm the three tables are marked Queryable and Artifact Snapshot Gate is PASS. In NL2SQL QA, ask: List all singer names in concerts in year 2014. Compare the generated SQL and result below with the Spider gold SQL. Check the selected names and duplicate rows; do not compare only whether both queries execute.

From Schema → CSV data, choose or drop the three downloaded files together. The table list below the upload area shows CSV tables already owned by the current project. Upload entry point in the project. The example project already contains the three Spider tables, each marked Queryable. Click Review CSV before creating anything. The preview shows each file's row count, proposed table name, normalized PostgreSQL column names, inferred types, and sample values. In this screenshot the same-named tables already exist, so the UI correctly reports that they cannot be overwritten. Delete the existing tables first if you want to repeat the import in this project. Review the inferred schema and sample data before import. The existing-name warning is expected for this already-imported project. The importer normalizes the headers to PostgreSQL-safe names. For example, Singer_ID becomes singer_id, and Song_release_year becomes song_release_year.

The local POC run generated: SELECT DISTINCT s.name FROM singer s JOIN singer_in_concert sic ON s.singer_id = sic.singer_id JOIN concert c ON sic.concert_id = c.concert_id WHERE c.year = 2014 ORDER BY s.name; It returned five unique names: John Nizinik, Justin Brown, Rose White, Timbaland, and Tribal King. The set of names matches Spider's gold result, but the row multiplicity differs: Spider returns Justin Brown twice while the generated SQL's DISTINCT returns it once. The generated query also sorts the result; Spider's gold SQL does not specify an order. The local app shows execution status, generated SQL, and returned rows together, so the result can be compared with the Spider gold query above. This is a one-question result comparison, not an official Spider benchmark score. A full benchmark run requires evaluating the benchmark split against its databases using Spider's evaluator; this page demonstrates how one uploaded CSV example can be traced from source data to gold SQL and compared with the local NL2SQL output.

Spider 1.0 is a human-labeled cross-domain Text-to-SQL benchmark. The official release documents the question, SQL, database ID, and schema formats in its GitHub repository. The archive mirror labels the dataset CC BY-SA 4.0 and attributes the source to the canonical Yale distribution. Please cite Tao Yu et al., “Spider: A Large-Scale Human-Labeled Dataset for Complex and Cross-Domain Semantic Parsing and Text-to-SQL Task,” EMNLP 2018. This page's CSVs are derived from the official concert_singer SQLite database, and the gold question/SQL are from its official dev.json development split.

Updated: 2026-10-17 Use the Start guide to import one small model and confirm it in the ER diagram. This guide uses one table: CREATE TABLE public.fund_master ( fund_code text PRIMARY KEY, fund_name text NOT NULL, risk_level integer, nav numeric(12,4), launched_on date );
Open Modeling and start the guide. In the Import panel, click DDL. Choose DDL in the Import panel.
The guide fills the DDL editor with fund_master. The preview must show: 1 model 5 columns 0 relationships When the preview is valid, Import is enabled. Review the parsed model before importing.
Click Import and wait for the success message: Imported 1 model(s) and 0 relationship(s).

The Modeling page switches to ER diagram. Confirm that: the Models panel contains one table: fund_master; the table node shows five columns; fund_code is marked as the primary key; the node shows zero links. The imported model is visible in the ER diagram. warning Import updates the project's draft modeling state. It does not make the model active for Ask/NL2SQL. Use Publish to continue to the artifact snapshot workflow.

From Active Snapshot, click Publish. Start the publish flow from Active Snapshot. Review the draft comparison, then click Publish in the review modal. Review the draft before publishing. Confirm the publish action. The dialog explains that the snapshot is activated for live use. Confirm publication and activation.

After the snapshot is published and activated, open the local NL2SQL QA route: /ai-nl2sql/nl2sql-qa?projectId=demo In Try It Out, enter: How many funds are there in total? Click Send to run the question against the active model. Ask the first question after activation. After Send completes, confirm the response card shows Success, a confidence score, and the generated SQL. In the local SQL-only demo, Rows 0 / 0 is expected because no business rows are connected; this step verifies the model-to-SQL response. For an executable Query DB project, continue with Understand the Thought Chain to review the full Copilot Ask Thought Chain and each validation/correction occurrence. Review the final response and generated SQL. warning If the page shows No active snapshot yet, finish publishing and activation before submitting the question.
Created: 2026-10-12 · Updated: 2026-10-12 Use Diagnostics to check shared services and one project's Active Snapshot. Run QA Smoke separately when you want to make one real Ask.

Select the project in the top bar. Choose Runtime Status in the left navigation to open Diagnostics. Click Refresh report. It checks system health and the selected project's runtime and Active Snapshot. It does not run QA Smoke. Review System Health, Current Project, and the project checks. Confirm the project reports QA available before trying a question. Only when you want a real Ask, click Run QA Smoke. It sends one project-scoped question and may call the configured LLM. The screenshots use the isolated poc_csv_reset project as an example. Select your own project when following these steps. Refresh report checks readiness. The separate QA Smoke card shows that no Ask has run yet. Readiness passed while QA Smoke remains not run. You can continue to Try Ask when ready.

These commands call the FastAPI backend directly. Change API_BASE if your backend uses another address. Each command prints the HTTP status and the complete JSON response; no jq is needed. Keep -f off so a structured error body remains visible. The health response samples below are abbreviated outputs from the mock API; the equity project examples intentionally show the state before it has an Active Snapshot. The MCP samples are from the live equity project, and request-specific values vary.

GET /api/health is the lightweight liveness check. It checks that the backend responds; it does not probe dependencies or run QA. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' curl -sS -i "${API_BASE}/api/health" Response sample and meaning HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json {"status":"ok","service":"bdd-nl2sql-backend-py"} status: ok confirms the backend listener responds. This endpoint does not prove that providers, a project, or QA are ready.

This checks shared dependencies, including the chat and embedding providers. It can make provider calls, so use it as an operator diagnostic rather than a cheap liveness probe. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' curl -sS -i -X POST "${API_BASE}/api/health?mode=system" Response sample and meaning { "mode": "system", "status": "ready", "system": { "status": "ready", "readyCount": 4, "partialCount": 0, "blockedCount": 0, "requiredCount": 4, "checks": [ {"key": "system-database", "status": "ready"}, {"key": "llm-provider", "status": "ready"}, {"key": "embedding-provider", "status": "ready"}, {"key": "vector-query-capability", "status": "ready"} ] }, "errors": [] } This is an abbreviated successful mock response. system.checks[] gives the individual dependency results; errors summarizes required blockers. Values and diagnostic details vary by environment.

Set PROJECT_ID to a registered project. This checks the selected project's Active Snapshot and runtime prerequisites; it does not send an Ask. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' PROJECT_ID='equity' curl -sS -i -X POST "${API_BASE}/api/health?mode=project&projectId=${PROJECT_ID}" Response sample and meaning { "mode": "project", "status": "setup", "project": { "projectId": "equity", "status": "setup", "qaAvailable": false, "runtime": { "status": "blocked", "readyCount": 1, "blockedCount": 2, "requiredCount": 3, "checks": [ { "key": "active-artifact-proof", "status": "blocked", "reasonCode": "active-snapshot-missing", "nextAction": "Publish or import a snapshot before running QA." } ] } }, "errors": [ {"check": "active-artifact-proof", "reasonCode": "active-snapshot-missing"} ] } This abbreviated mock response is HTTP 200 with a business status of setup: the project has no Active Snapshot yet. Read reasonCode and nextAction; HTTP 200 alone does not mean the project is QA-ready.
documents.s: Is this project's Active Snapshot ready for QA?

documents.t: Run this only when you want to call the project's configured Ask tool. It may call the LLM and reports the attempt in .smoke. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' PROJECT_ID='equity' curl -sS -i -X POST "${API_BASE}/api/health?mode=smoke&projectId=${PROJECT_ID}" Response sample and meaning { "mode": "smoke", "status": "failed", "smoke": { "status": "failed", "projectId": "equity", "question": "count", "summary": "QA Smoke could not resolve the MCP Ask tool.", "details": "No active artifact version available. Open /copilot-ask/artifact-version and create or activate one first." }, "errors": [ {"check": "qa-smoke", "summary": "QA Smoke could not resolve the MCP Ask tool."} ] } This abbreviated mock response shows a Smoke attempt that cannot start because the project has no Active Snapshot. After prerequisites pass, .smoke.ask contains the actual Ask call result; a failed attempt is reported and does not change the Active Snapshot.
documents.s: Do one real QA Smoke Ask

documents.t: mode=full checks shared services, visits projects serially, and may run one Smoke Ask for each project whose prerequisites are ready. It is an operator report, not a liveness or readiness probe. This request intentionally has no PROJECT_ID. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' curl -sS -i -X POST "${API_BASE}/api/health?mode=full" Response sample and meaning { "mode": "full", "status": "failed", "system": {"status": "ready"}, "projects": { "equity": { "projectId": "equity", "status": "setup", "qaAvailable": false, "qaSmoke": { "status": "not_run", "summary": "Project prerequisites failed; QA Smoke was not run." } } }, "errors": [ {"projectId": "equity", "check": "active-artifact-proof", "reasonCode": "active-snapshot-missing"} ] } This abbreviated mock response uses projects as a map keyed by project ID. The project is not ready, so its qaSmoke.status is not_run; a ready project may receive a real Smoke attempt. Read the JSON status and check results as well as the HTTP status. A completed diagnostic can return HTTP 200 while its JSON reports failed, partial, or setup.

Use tools/list to discover the exact tool name configured for the selected project's Active Snapshot. Then call the tool with the same value in the Mcp-Name header and params.name. The example below uses equity_saerch_test and the question shown in its response sample. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' PROJECT_ID='equity' curl -sS -N --max-time 30 "${API_BASE}/mcp/${PROJECT_ID}/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \ -H 'Mcp-Method: tools/list' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"},"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}' tools/list response sample and meaning { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "tools": [ {"name": "equity_ask"}, {"name": "equity_saerch_test"} ], "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "NL2SQL MCP Server - equity", "version": "1.0.0" } } } } This is an abbreviated excerpt from the live equity response; each tool also has a description and inputSchema. Use the returned name for the next request, not the description or prefix. Call the equity_saerch_test tool for a custom question. This is a real Ask and may call the configured LLM. The JSON-RPC params key is spelled exactly as shown; this stateless request does not need initialize or Mcp-Session-Id. API_BASE='http://127.0.0.1:4000' PROJECT_ID='equity' TOOL_NAME='equity_saerch_test' curl -sS -N --max-time 120 "${API_BASE}/mcp/${PROJECT_ID}/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \ -H 'Mcp-Method: tools/call' \ -H "Mcp-Name: ${TOOL_NAME}" \ -d "{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"${TOOL_NAME}","arguments":{"query":"How many core business records are there?"},"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"},"io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}" tools/call response sample and meaning The actual call returned 1446 for the question. This response excerpt omits generated IDs and long reasoning text: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "result": { "resultType": "complete", "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "{
 "status": "success",
 "confidence": 0.9,
 "query": "How many core business records are there?",
 "results": [{"core_business_record_count": 1446}],
 "sql": "SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT fund_code) AS core_business_record_count FROM fund_master_view;",
 ..." } ], "isError": false, "structuredContent": { "status": "success", "bundleHash": "<Active Snapshot hash>", "confidence": 0.9, "query": "How many core business records are there?", "results": [{"core_business_record_count": 1446}], "sql": "SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT fund_code) AS core_business_record_count FROM fund_master_view;", "meta": {"mode": "SQL_EXECUTE_RESULT", "timing": {"totalDurationMs": 19939}}, "reason": {"answer": "<answer explanation>", "business": "<business reasoning>", "technical": "<technical analysis>"}, "queryId": "<generated query ID>", "threadId": "<generated thread ID>", "traceId": "<generated trace ID>", "suggestedQuestion": ["<follow-up question>"], "groundReason": "<grounding explanation>" }, "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": { "name": "NL2SQL MCP Server - equity", "version": "1.0.0" } } } } content[0].text is a string containing the historical NL2SQL business JSON; structuredContent is the machine-readable object for clients that support it. resultType: complete and isError: false describe the MCP call, while structuredContent.status: success and results describe the NL2SQL answer. The generated IDs, hash, SQL and answer vary by request and Active Snapshot.
documents.s: Call the project's MCP tool directly

documents.t: What you see Inspect Next check Backend does not respond HTTP status and connection error Confirm the backend is running and API_BASE points to its address. System Health is not ready .system.checks[] and .errors[] Find checks whose status is not ready; read summary, details, reasonCode, and nextAction when present. Project is setup or not ready .project.status, .project.qaAvailable, .project.runtime.checks[], and .project.errors[] Locate the failed or blocked runtime check and follow its details and nextAction. QA Smoke failed .smoke.status, .smoke.ask.status, .smoke.ask.errorCode, and .smoke.ask.details Review the Ask error and provider/runtime details. Smoke is one real Ask attempt; it does not replace the Active Snapshot. Draft and Active may differ Response from GET /api/artifact-versions/freshness?projectId=… Inspect the freshness result, then review the Snapshot diff before publishing. For the complete request and response contract, see Health and Readiness APIs. For deployment probes, keep inexpensive process liveness separate from dependency readiness and real QA work. See the official Kubernetes probe guidance and Microsoft health-check guidance.
The repository contains separate backend and frontend development commands. Use the repository scripts and the environment examples instead of inventing local runtime values.
cd src/backend_py source .venv/bin/activate python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 4000
cd src/frontend npm ci npm run dev:python

The documentation site is independent from the application runtime. The private repository's docs-site/ is the only editable source. The local 20260416-nl2sql-docs path is a symlink to that same working tree; its independent public Git metadata is stored beside the private repository, not inside the shared files. Run these commands from the private repository root: ./script/docs-publish.sh check git status --short -- docs-site git -C "$(pwd)/20260416-nl2sql-docs" \ --git-dir="$(pwd)/../20260416-nl2sql-docs.git" \ --work-tree="$(pwd)/20260416-nl2sql-docs" status --short For local documentation work, edit only docs-site/ and use its normal commands: cd docs-site npm ci npm run start npm run build Publish the same working tree through the two independent Git repositories with one explicit command: cd .. ./script/docs-publish.sh publish "docs: describe the documentation change" The command verifies the shared tree, pushes the private repository, pushes public main, builds the site, deploys public gh-pages, and verifies the public URL. It stops at the first failed stage; it does not reconcile a second source tree or reuse either repository's Git metadata. To tear down the local sharing layout, stop publication first, remove the 20260416-nl2sql-docs symlink, restore the public working tree from the migration backup, and move the sidecar 20260416-nl2sql-docs.git metadata back into the restored public repository. Do not delete either Git metadata store while the shared path is active. In GitHub repository settings, set Pages to Deploy from a branch, select gh-pages, and select the repository root (/). The configured url, baseUrl, and deployment branch must match the public repository.

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health curl -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=project&projectId=equity' | jq .project warning Do not use a successful HTTP process check as proof that a project can execute Ask/NL2SQL. Use the project Runtime Readiness and QA Smoke results.

This project provides a knowledge-grounded NL2SQL runtime for project-scoped data sources. The active artifact snapshot is the versioned runtime boundary for prompts, knowledge, SQL examples, instructions, schema materialization, and runtime policies.

Component Responsibility React/Vite frontend Dashboard, modeling, artifact review, QA, and Copilot Ask UI FastAPI backend Runtime APIs, LangGraph execution, MCP, readiness, and artifact lifecycle Control-plane PostgreSQL Artifact metadata, runtime bindings, QA history, and observability state Query-side PostgreSQL Business tables and views queried by generated SQL LLM/embedding providers SQL reasoning, answer generation, and retrieval embeddings
Read the NL2SQL pipeline. Review RAG and few-shot evidence. Run the local stack using Local Development. Use the Runtime Readiness API before debugging a query.

Created October 7, 2026 · Last updated October 17, 2026 Use the application's Guide to take a project from CSV files to a verified NL2SQL answer. The same seven steps appear in Guide and are exercised by the mock Playwright E2E. Screenshots below are captured by that E2E run and published here from the same image buffers. The captures use the isolated poc_csv_reset project; select your own project in the upper-right picker. It must use POC_CSV_SQL_EXECUTE_RESULT mode and have a writable Query DB. See Local Development to start the app. Download these sample CSV files into one folder before starting: Download singer.csv Download concert.csv Download singer_in_concert.csv
documents.s: Import CSV data and run your first QA

documents.t: On Artifact → Schema, confirm the project picker shows your project. Open Guide in the lower-left corner, choose Schema & QA → Import schema, then click the highlighted Import button. Opening the source picker does not change project data. The guide then highlights CSV data · POC; CSV model metadata does not upload query rows. Open Guide from the lower-left corner. Choose Schema & QA to get started, Thought Chain to explore an answer, or Snapshot to manage configuration. Each entry opens its own guide. Start Import schema from the Schema page. Choose CSV data · POC as the import source. Select the downloaded CSV files. Confirm that all three files are listed, then choose Review CSV.

The preview proposes tables named singer, concert, and singer_in_concert. Select each file and review its table name, columns, data types, and sample values. Fix any issue before continuing. If you open this step before uploading files, Guide explains the prerequisite and keeps Continue unavailable. Review every proposed table and column before creating schema.

The confirmation stage summarizes 3 tables · 22 rows. Check the table names and row counts, then click Create schema. This imports the CSV rows and creates a Draft. A Draft is not yet available to QA; it does not become Active until you publish it. Opening Create schema before a valid CSV preview shows the prerequisite and disables creation. Confirm the import summary and create the Draft.

After creation, the Schema page shows the imported models. Click Deploy to open Active Snapshot and inspect the Draft. Deploy opens the snapshot workspace; the Draft is still unpublished at this point. Open Active Snapshot to review the Draft.

On Active Snapshot, select Publish. Review the changes in the first dialog, then confirm Publish in the final dialog. Wait for Current Snapshot to show Active and Guide to say Your data is ready. This is the point where the imported data becomes available to QA. Start Publish from Active Snapshot. Review the Draft before confirming. Confirm Publish. Continue after the snapshot has become Active.

Open Check readiness from Guide. On Diagnostics, click Refresh report and wait for the project health check. Guide advances only when runtime readiness reports ready. This health check is different from QA Smoke: it checks project and Active Snapshot readiness but does not submit the example question. Run the health check from Diagnostics. Proceed when Guide confirms readiness passed.

Choose Go to Try Ask. In NL2SQL QA Console, submit this question and wait for the result: List all singer names in concerts in year 2014. Ask a question against the Active Snapshot. The example should return Success, 6 rows, the singer names, and generated SQL. Justin Brown appears twice. Guide completes only after the application returns a successful QA result. The answer was generated from the published CSV tables. To clear the project and repeat the exercise, follow Reset a project.

Created October 7, 2026 · Last updated October 8, 2026 Reset returns an editable project to its first-use state. It removes its Active Snapshot, draft, model, Knowledge, Instructions, Schema RAG, project QA/Chat/API history, and uploaded POC CSV tables. The project entry and connection settings remain. QA is unavailable until you publish new data or import a valid snapshot. The screenshots use the isolated poc_csv_reset project and the three files from Import CSV data and run your first QA. Select your project in the upper-right picker. Keep your original CSV files if you plan to upload them again. IMPORT_DIR projects can also Reset after backing up Active. Reset preserves the configured package and ownership; restart to import that package again. Keep the required external query data available.

In the left menu, open Artifact → Configuration. The page title is Active Snapshot. Check the project picker and Current Snapshot · Active, then locate Reset project next to Export. Confirm the project and Active Snapshot before selecting Reset project.

Click Reset project. The app first exports and validates the current Active Snapshot, downloads a ZIP named after the export folder, then opens the confirmation dialog. Keep the downloaded ZIP. The dialog displays the exact folder name; Reset is disabled until you enter it. The export succeeded; Reset is still disabled while the confirmation field is empty. If the Pod's export directory is permission-denied or read-only, the backend logs WARN and skips only server disk saving. The ZIP still downloads automatically, and the dialog shows Server disk save skipped. Keep the downloaded archive: no server-side backup was saved. Reset verifies the complete downloaded package against the still-current Active; it does not require a writable export directory. Other failures, including disk-full or invalid export content, still block Reset. If the project has no Active Snapshot, Reset does not export or download anything. It opens a cleanup confirmation without a folder-name input so unpublished content, history and owned CSV tables can still be removed. The server rechecks Active absence under the project lock; if Active appeared meanwhile, Reset is rejected. This is not an automatic deletion on opening the dialog.

Read the deletion list. When Active was exported, type the export folder name shown in the dialog exactly into the confirmation field. Check that Reset project becomes enabled, then click it. Do not type the ZIP filename with .zip or invent a name. With no Active, simply review the deletion scope and confirm Reset; no backup name is required. Enter the folder name from this export, then confirm Reset. A wrong name cannot start Reset. If Active changed after export, export that current snapshot again before resetting. Existing runtime or Publish-status warnings do not disable Reset; the backup and project cleanup must still complete successfully.
documents.s: 3. Confirm the folder name and Reset

documents.t: After Reset, Configuration shows No active snapshot, No tables to publish, and Guide with 0 of 7 Schema/QA steps complete. Open NL2SQL QA Console: it says Publish your data to start asking questions. A question cannot reach the MCP tool without an Active Snapshot. The project is back at initial setup, with no Active Snapshot or model. QA reports that data must be published before questions can run.

Open Artifact → Schema and import the original three CSV files again. Follow the Import → Review CSV → Create schema stages in the CSV import guide. The preview should list singer, concert, and singer_in_concert without table-name conflicts. Confirm 3 tables · 22 rows, then click Create schema. The same files and table names are available again after Reset. Confirm the recreated tables. The three tables now appear in Schema, but they are Pending Publish and QA still has no Active Snapshot. Import creates unpublished content.
documents.s: 5. Upload the same CSV files again

documents.t: Click Deploy, then on Configuration review the Unpublished changes and click Publish. Complete the review and confirmation dialogs as shown in the CSV import guide. Wait until Current Snapshot · Active appears. The new snapshot contains the reimported model; Knowledge and Instructions removed by Reset do not return merely because you uploaded the same CSV files. The reimported model is ready for Publish. Publish restores an Active Snapshot for the project.

Open NL2SQL QA Console and ask List all singer names in concerts in year 2014. for these sample files. Confirm Success, 6 rows, and the generated SQL. QA uses the new Active Snapshot after Publish. The exported ZIP preserves the old snapshot configuration. To import it later, first restore any Query DB tables and rows it requires; the snapshot export does not replace the CSV data you originally uploaded.

Created: 2026-10-17 · Updated: 2026-10-17 The Thought Chain explains how your question becomes an answer: understanding, knowledge and instruction retrieval, schema selection, planning, SQL generation, validation, any corrections, execution, and answer rendering. Open NL2SQL QA → Copilot Ask, choose your project, then open Guide → Thought Chain. All steps always shows the complete navigation in one vertical list. There is no expand or collapse control. Use it to jump to a stage, or use Next to follow them in order. The highlighted area is the actual control or evidence for the selected question. Opening the Guide does not run another question or correction. Every executed step can contain: Input Context: what that step received. Thinking: model-provided reasoning, when available. An absent lane means none was supplied. Output: what that step produced, including its actual error if it failed. JSON controls: structured details for the corresponding input or output. Expand them or use Copy JSON when you need the complete evidence. Completed describes that stage only. A generated SQL candidate can still fail validation. Earlier failures stay visible even when the final answer succeeds. Not executed for this ask means the stage did not run, rather than implying success. The following screenshots use the passing scenario 03 mock E2E, with controlled model responses and a real PostgreSQL query database. Its missing-column error is deliberately arranged in test fixtures; ordinary questions do not have to fail. The correction example requires executable database mode. The SQL-only import tutorial demonstrates generation without executing business rows.

Enter a question and submit it with the arrow button. The selected project's Active Snapshot supplies the business context. In the isolated mock example, enter: Count funds and verify SQL correction recovery. Expected: the question appears in the conversation and its actual execution steps become available. Start with the project and question you want to investigate.

Select Understanding under All steps. Explain what you are asking before searching for data. Input Context: Your question and conversation context. Output: The interpreted question and selected intent. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Explain what you are asking before searching for data.

Select SQL Pair RAG under All steps. Find relevant question–SQL examples in project knowledge. Input Context: The question used to search knowledge. Output: Retrieved examples and their relevance. No matches is a valid result. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Find relevant question–SQL examples in project knowledge.

Select User Instructions under All steps. Find the project instructions that apply to this question. Input Context: The question and instruction context. Output: Selected business rules that guide the answer. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Find the project instructions that apply to this question.

Select Schema Linking under All steps. Identify the tables and columns needed for the question. Input Context: The question and available schema context. Output: The selected schema and relationships used to write SQL. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Identify the tables and columns needed for the question.

Select Reasoning under All steps. In normal mode, plan how to answer the question. Input Context: The question, schema, examples, and applicable instructions. Output: The query plan used by Generating. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. In normal mode, plan how to answer the question.

Select Generating under All steps. In normal mode, turn the plan into a SQL candidate. Input Context: The query plan and its supporting context. Output: The complete generated SQL. It still needs validation. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. In normal mode, turn the plan into a SQL candidate.

Select Reason and Generate under All steps. In Fast mode, planning and generation run together. This replaces the separate Reasoning and Generating stages. Input Context: The question, schema, examples, and applicable instructions. Output: The query plan and complete SQL candidate. The mock example initially produces SELECT missing_column FROM fund_master_view. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. In Fast mode, planning and generation run together. This replaces the separate Reasoning and Generating stages.

Select Validating under All steps. Check whether the SQL is valid before running it. Select Check 1 · Failed to inspect the initial failure. Input Context: The exact SQL, attempt number, and validation mode. In this example, attempt is 0 and mode is explain. Output: The verdict and original error. PostgreSQL reports column "missing_column" does not exist; Output JSON retains isValid: false and outcome: "error". Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Check whether the SQL is valid before running it. Select Check 1 · Failed to inspect the initial failure.

Select Correcting under All steps. Use the validation error to produce a new candidate. Read the previous SQL alongside the error before inspecting the new SQL. Input Context: The previous SQL, original error, and retry budget. Output: The corrected candidate or actual correction failure. Here the model returns SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_funds FROM fund_master_view. A completed correction does not mean the candidate has passed validation. Expected: the highlighted step shows this question's actual evidence and stage status. Use the validation error to produce a new candidate. Read the previous SQL alongside the error before inspecting the new SQL. Return to Validating and choose Check 2 · Passed. Confirm that the corrected COUNT statement passed its own database validation at attempt 1. Each additional check retains its own SQL and verdict; the first failure remains failed. Verify the candidate in a separate validation check. When no correction is needed, Correcting says Not executed for this ask. If the allowed corrections are exhausted, select Retry limit · Failed in Correcting. The ask ends with Exceeded correction retries, retains the preceding diagnostics, and does not claim a successful answer. A zero budget allows no correction model calls. A failed run retains its error and earlier attempts.

Select SQL Execution. This stage runs the validated SQL against the project's query database. Input Context: the SQL actually sent for execution. Output: the returned rows and columns, or the original execution error. Expected: the controlled example returns one row containing total_funds: 1446. Your project's data determines its own result. Check the executed SQL and returned data.

Select Answer Rendering. This stage turns the verified result into the answer shown in the conversation. Input Context: the question, executed SQL, and returned data. Output: the user-facing answer and supporting result. Expected: the final answer agrees with the executed result. Generation alone does not prove the answer was executed successfully. Connect the final answer to its supporting data.

Close the Guide and reopen the question from conversation history. Refresh the page, then select Guide → Thought Chain → All steps → Reopen history. Expected: the question retains the same steps, failed SQL, correction candidates, original errors, and final result. Editing Draft later does not rewrite this completed run. Visiting the Guide does not mark this verification complete. Return to the original execution evidence at any time.

Run bash script/e2e-mock/03_run_non_json_error.sh for the focused scenario or bash script/e2e-mock/99_run_all_e2e-and-report.sh for the full mock suite. The scenario verifies API-to-DOM evidence, JSON copy, real correction, exhaustion, zero budget, normal/Fast success, refresh/history, and Snapshot preservation. Each image uses the identical PNG attached to its Monocart report. The complete image set is published only after the scenario passes; a failed run preserves approved images.

Created: 2026-10-11 · Updated: 2026-10-11 Open Guide → Snapshot. Select any step to find its existing control; you can start at Export when an Active Snapshot already exists. Snapshot is the authority for NL2SQL configuration. It carries models, knowledge, runtime policies, MCP tools, and Prompt files. The database stores the environment's runtime data. Snapshot and Schema/QA have separate Guide entries.
documents.s: Export, edit and import a Snapshot

documents.t: In UAT, review the Draft and click Publish. It becomes Active and its ZIP downloads automatically. New QA uses this Active Snapshot. To rebuild runtime without changing business content, choose Current Active Snapshot in the same Publish dialog. This preserves a different Unpublished Draft. Runtime warnings do not disable recovery; an actual build failure is reported and does not replace the committed source. Re-Publish rebuilds runtime from the selected business Snapshot.
Click Export to download the current Active package. You do not need to Publish again. Unpack the ZIP to inspect or edit the files. Export downloads the current Active package.
Select a file in Configuration → Active Snapshot → Unpublished changes. Click Field mapping beside its filename. The application opens the file’s existing UI and shows the shared Guide popup there.

Choose semantic/modeling-state.json, then Field mapping. In Schema, choose the model and column. The Guide shows that record’s Draft JSON and points to the corresponding real Columns field. Click a key or use Previous / Next to switch fields. Snapshot key Schema field models[].columns[].name Name models[].columns[].alias Alias models[].columns[].dataType Type models[].columns[].description Description models[].columns[].isPrimaryKey PK tag; false means no tag

Choose knowledge/sql-pairs.json, then Field mapping. In Knowledge, select the record. Its ID locates the actual row, including when the record was not on the initial table page. Snapshot key Knowledge field [].question Matching question [].sql SQL statement [].is_enabled Enabled [].provenance Source; manual displays Manual
knowledge/instructions.json is marked Beta function · ignored. Field mapping for Instructions is not included in this Guide; its existing feature and Snapshot import/export remain available.

A file in prompts/ opens the corresponding System or User prompt in Prompt workspace. Prompt files are TXT, not JSON. Snapshot View shows all prompt content; Export includes the actual saved TXT files and their exact whitespace; absent files are not synthesized from templates. The example below uses a prompt edited and saved through the real UI before Publish. config/portable-environment-agnostic-config.json opens Diagnostics → Effective configuration → Active runtime policies. Select a key to locate its real policy field. config/mcp-tools.json opens NL2SQL QA → API Info. Choose a tool to compare its description with the actual tool description. Its annotations control visible tool hints; inputSchema defines the arguments shown by View Schema. knowledge/logical-views.json opens Semantic Views in Schema. Select a record to locate its Name, Description and read-only SQL statement. Empty files show No records in this file, without inventing an example record. manifest.json describes the package format and file paths. semantic/business-metadata.json holds business labels, descriptions, tags and value options. Their existing viewing surface is the Snapshot viewer; they have no separate business-field editor. The popup labels its JSON Unpublished Draft. Active content and Active-only UI surfaces can differ. Business names and values identify configuration; system IDs are not exported. Created time is audit information and is not an exported field. Guide navigation does not edit, save or publish content. Return to Snapshot preserves the selected file; close the popup or press Escape to continue normal work.

In View → Hash content, select a file to inspect the exact business fields used by diff and SHA-256. Copy the complete canonical input to independently recompute the fingerprint. Excluded fields show their file path and reason. A stored hash mismatch is displayed without rewriting the binding. Expected system IDs, audit fields and standard package metadata are informational exclusions; normal Export and Import do not show warnings. In Import, click package metadata fields excluded from business content to expand the exact excluded paths and reasons; this section starts collapsed and also supports Enter. Business Schema fields determine what is imported; arbitrary undeclared fields/files are ignored with a warning summary and expandable details. Import logs WARN with every ignored path and reason. Indexed records (items/order) are read as business records, retaining valid business order; system identity is not an import prerequisite. Unparseable business content, ambiguous references and unsafe archives stop import before any data is replaced. Runtime readiness is checked separately; provider failures do not disable configuration transfer.

Edit the corresponding files using your own editor. Preserve business names, unrelated values, and business order. System IDs and audit metadata are informational exclusions. ZIP the complete Snapshot folder, including manifest.json, config/, knowledge/, semantic/, and prompts/. Include unchanged files and all files in the original export, including those not described by the Normal view.

Open the target environment's project. Choose Active Snapshot → Import and upload the ZIP or full folder. Validation runs automatically; click Import after it reports OK. Valid business content becomes the selected Active Snapshot before runtime synchronization. If synchronization fails, the response explains why; that same Active content remains available in View and Export. Health and QA report the failure until its matching runtime is rebuilt.
In Diagnostics, click Refresh report. Confirm readiness is ready and QA available is shown.
In NL2SQL QA, send a representative question and check its SQL, answer, and result.

The same package can be imported through POST /api/artifact-versions/import-upload, or from a server-accessible folder through POST /api/artifact-versions/import. Startup import uses PROJECT_<ID>_ARTIFACT_ACTIVE_SNAPSHOT_IMPORT_DIR. These are existing deployment options. Snapshot export/import does not move runtime table rows or perform DDL/data migrations. The target environment must provide the required datasource, business objects, and access for readiness and QA to pass. The actual application Guide defines this journey. e2e/mock-poc-csv-reset.spec.ts, run by script/e2e-mock/11_run_poc_csv_reset.sh in the 99 suite, verifies the same controls, edited ZIP import, Active content, readiness, and expected QA result. After the whole journey passes, the same screenshot buffers are attached to Monocart and copied to this docs-site.

An active artifact snapshot is the versioned runtime boundary for prompts, SQL pairs, user instructions, semantic models, schema RAG, MCP tools, and runtime policies. The snapshot gate compares draft and active truth. Publishing and activation are the promotion boundary; normal Ask/NL2SQL execution must not combine draft content with an older active runtime. Draft changes ↓ publish Artifact version ↓ activate Active snapshot + runtime materialization ↓ readiness + QA Smoke Servable project runtime

QA Smoke is an explicit business check. It runs one real project-scoped MCP ask against the current Active Snapshot. Opening the page, refreshing Health, publishing, and startup do not run it. curl --max-time 120 -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=smoke&projectId=equity' | jq '.smoke' passed means the Ask completed. failed includes an executed Ask error such as provider 429 or timeout. not_run means a prerequisite such as an Active Snapshot was missing. The attempt records its time and actual bundleHash when available; it does not change project availability or Active content. For all projects, call synchronous mode=full manually inside a Pod with a suitable client timeout.

Operation Meaning GET /api/health Listener is alive; no dependency probes POST /api/health?mode=system Shared DB, chat provider, embedding, and pgvector currently work POST /api/health?mode=project&projectId=<id> Selected Active Snapshot and query-side DB are usable; no LLM call POST /api/health?mode=smoke&projectId=<id> One actual business Ask attempt POST /api/health?mode=full Manual serial inspection of all projects Before listening, startup runs the shared system checker internally at most ten times and then converges configured IMPORT_DIR snapshots. Exhausted system grace or configured import failure exits code 1. A project without Active and without IMPORT_DIR remains available for initial setup. Provider 429 during a later manual Smoke is an attempt failure, not a persistent process or Active state.

Before listening, the backend checks shared DB, chat provider, embedding, and pgvector through the same internal checker as mode=system. It tries at most ten times within STARTUP_FAIL_FAST_GRACE_SECONDS, logging each failed dependency. Exhausted grace exits code 1. Success proceeds immediately to configured IMPORT_DIR snapshot convergence; an invalid configured import also exits non-zero with its project cause. Startup does not run QA Smoke. Projects without IMPORT_DIR and without an Active Snapshot can start for first-time authoring; their mode=project status is setup until Publish or Import succeeds. A failed runtime Publish leaves the previous Active available. Use lightweight GET /api/health for liveness after startup. Operators may inspect POST /api/health?mode=system or a selected mode=project without asking a QA question. Invoke mode=smoke or synchronous mode=full manually when a real business check is needed. mode=full is not a Kubernetes probe.

If the process exits during boot, inspect its final log entry. It identifies the failed shared dependency and attempt number, or the configured IMPORT_DIR project and content error. System health is retried up to ten times within the grace budget; a configured import error exits non-zero. After the listener starts, inspect current layers separately: curl -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=system' | jq '.system, .errors' curl -sS -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/health?mode=project&projectId=equity' | jq '.project' No Active Snapshot is a project setup state: Publish or Import one before QA. A business DB or Active material failure appears in .project.errors with a reason code and next action. Provider 429 during manual mode=smoke is only that attempt's failure; inspect .smoke and retry when the provider recovers.
